front: Name the specific class of antimicrobial agents classically linked to the development of Stevens-Johnson Syndrome according to the provided pharmacology text.
back:
• Sulfonamides
• Includes drugs like Sulfamethoxazole
• Reaction occurs in <1% of treatment courses.

category: Describe mechanism of action, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Beta-lactam antibiotics are structural analogs of the natural [___] substrate and covalently bind to the active site of penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs) to inhibit cell wall synthesis.
back: d-Alanyl-d-Alanine (d-Ala-d-Alanine)

category: Describe mechanism of action, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: A patient receiving a rapid intravenous infusion of Vancomycin suddenly develops intense flushing, pruritus, and an erythematous rash over the face, neck, and upper torso. This reaction is primarily mediated by the release of [___].
back: Histamine (resulting in "Red Man Syndrome")

category: Describe mechanism of action, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Explain the biological mechanism of action of Daptomycin and identify the primary reason for its lack of efficacy in treating bacterial pneumonia.
back:
• Binds cell membrane via calcium-dependent insertion of lipid tail, causing depolarization and potassium efflux.
• Inactivated by pulmonary surfactant, rendering it ineffective in lung tissue.

category: Describe mechanism of action, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Contrast Ciprofloxacin and Moxifloxacin regarding their clinical utility in treating Pseudomonas aeruginosa infections and their role in managing urinary tract infections (UTIs).
back:
• Ciprofloxacin: Strong anti-pseudomonal activity; high renal excretion makes it a drug of choice for UTIs.
• Moxifloxacin: No appreciable activity against Pseudomonas; primarily hepatically cleared with low urinary levels, making it unsuitable for UTIs.

category: Describe mechanism of action, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Identify the primary pharmacological mechanism by which Rifampin reduces the plasma concentration of drugs such as warfarin, methadone, and oral contraceptives.
back: Potent induction of multiple cytochrome P450 (CYP) isoforms (1A2, 2C9, 2C19, 2D6, 3A4), which significantly increases the hepatic elimination of these drugs.

category: Describe mechanism of action, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: The most common serious dose-related adverse effect of Ethambutol is [___], which typically presents as decreased visual acuity or red-green color blindness.
back: Retrobulbar neuritis (Optic neuritis)

category: Describe mechanism of action, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: A patient on Amphotericin B for Cryptococcal meningitis develops azotemia and severe hypokalemia. To attenuate the prerenal component of this medication's nephrotoxicity, the clinician should implement [___].
back: Sodium loading (administration of normal saline infusions before/with doses).

category: Describe mechanism of action, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Describe the mechanism by which Oseltamivir treats influenza infections and specify the critical therapeutic window for its initiation.
back:
• Competitively inhibits viral neuraminidase to prevent the release of progeny virions from infected host cells.
• Must be initiated within 48 hours of symptom onset to be effective.

category: Describe mechanism of action, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Contrast the fungal cell targets and specific biocidal effects of Amphotericin B versus the Echinocandin class (e.g., Caspofungin).
back:
• Amphotericin B: Binds ergosterol in the cell membrane to form pores, leading to leakage of ions.
• Echinocandins: Inhibit β(1–3)-glucan synthesis, disrupting the integrity of the fungal cell wall.

category: Describe mechanism of action, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Identify the metabolic interaction between Metronidazole and ethanol, and name the specific syndrome that results from their concurrent use.
back:
• Disulfiram-like reaction.
• Inhibition of aldehyde dehydrogenase leads to accumulation of acetaldehyde, causing nausea, vomiting, flushing, and tachycardia.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) is clinically defined as a severe mucocutaneous reaction involving skin detachment of less than [___]% of the total body surface area (TBSA).
back:
• Less than 10% TBSA skin detachment.
• 10-30% detachment is classified as SJS/TEN overlap.
• Greater than 30% is Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN).
• This classification is the primary UHS board prognostic standard.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: A patient started on Sulfamethoxazole 5 days ago presents with a 2-day history of high fever, sore throat, and severe conjunctivitis followed by the sudden appearance of painful, dusky-red skin macules. Identify this clinical stage.
back:
• Prodromal phase of SJS.
• Precedes cutaneous eruptions by 1-3 days.
• Characterized by systemic symptoms (flu-like illness).
• Ocular and oral symptoms often serve as early warning signs.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: Explain the diagnostic requirement regarding mucosal involvement in a patient suspected of having Stevens-Johnson Syndrome.
back:
• Involvement of at least two distinct mucosal sites.
• Affects the mouth, eyes, or urogenital tract in 90% of cases.
• Presents as painful hemorrhagic crusts, ulcers, or bullae.
• Can cause permanent scarring or symblepharon.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: Contrast SJS and Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS) regarding the level of epidermal cleavage and mucosal involvement.
back:
• SJS: Deep subepidermal cleavage at dermo-epidermal junction; mucosal involvement is present.
• SSSS: Superficial intraepidermal cleavage (granular layer); mucosal involvement is absent.
• Both exhibit a positive Nikolsky sign.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: Describe the morphology and distribution of the primary cutaneous lesions seen in the early eruptive phase of Stevens-Johnson Syndrome.
back:
• Atypical "targetoid" lesions (dusky centers with erythematous halos).
• Predominantly affects the face and trunk (centripetal distribution).
• Progresses to flaccid bullae and large sheets of denuded skin.
• Individual lesions are typically flat, not raised.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: The characteristic clinical finding of the epidermis detaching from the underlying dermis when lateral pressure is applied to the skin in SJS is known as the [___] sign.
back:
• Nikolsky Sign.
• Indicates poor cohesion between epidermal layers or dermo-epidermal junction.
• Essential for bedside assessment of blistering disorders.
• Found in SJS, TEN, and Pemphigus Vulgaris.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: An HIV-positive patient being treated with Nevirapine develops widespread painful skin rashes and oral ulcers. Which genetic screen should have been considered, and why is this patient at higher risk?
back:
• HLA-B*1502 or HLA-B*5701 screening.
• SJS risk is higher in HIV patients due to immune dysregulation.
• Nevirapine is a high-risk NNRTI trigger.
• Risk increases with high baseline CD4 counts in women.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: How does the cytotoxic T-cell response specifically lead to the massive epidermal sloughing observed in Stevens-Johnson Syndrome?
back:
• Widespread keratinocyte apoptosis via Type IV hypersensitivity.
• Release of Granulysin, a potent cytotoxic protein.
• Fas-Fas ligand interaction activates the death receptor pathway.
• Leads to full-thickness necrosis of the epidermis.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: Contrast SJS and Erythema Multiforme (EM) based on their typical etiologies and degree of systemic toxicity.
back:
• SJS: Primarily drug-induced (Sulfonamides, anticonvulsants); high systemic toxicity and mortality risk.
• EM: Primarily infection-induced (HSV, Mycoplasma); usually localized with minimal systemic involvement.
• EM shows typical "bullseye" targets; SJS shows atypical flat targets.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: Name the validated scoring system used within the first 24 hours of admission to predict the mortality rate of a patient with SJS.
back:
• SCORTEN (Score of Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis).
• Evaluates 7 independent variables (Age, Heart Rate, Glucose, etc.).
• Calculated to determine if intensive care or burn unit transfer is necessary.
• High scores correlate with greater than 90% mortality.

category: Describe mechanism of action, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: To prevent the inactivation of amoxicillin by bacterial enzymes, it is commonly co-formulated with [___], which acts as a suicide inhibitor of beta-lactamase.
back: Clavulanic acid (or Clavulanate).

category: Describe mechanism of action, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: A 45-year-old male treated with Cefotetan for an intra-abdominal infection develops severe flushing, tachycardia, and nausea after consuming alcohol. This reaction is primarily due to the drug's [___] side chain.
back:
• Methylthiotetrazole (MTT) group.
• This group inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, causing a disulfiram-like reaction.

category: Describe mechanism of action, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Explain the molecular mechanism by which Vancomycin inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis.
back:
• Binds firmly to the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of nascent peptidoglycan pentapeptide.
• Inhibits transglycosylase, preventing further elongation and cross-linking of the peptidoglycan.

category: Describe mechanism of action, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Contrast the mechanisms of action of Amphotericin B and Fluconazole regarding their effect on fungal ergosterol.
back:
• Amphotericin B: Forms artificial pores (ion channels) in the cell membrane by binding directly to ergosterol.
• Fluconazole: Inhibits 14-α-demethylase, preventing the synthesis of ergosterol from lanosterol.

category: Describe mechanism of action, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: State the pharmacological reason why Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) must be co-administered with Isoniazid (INH) during tuberculosis therapy.
back:
• INH promotes the renal excretion of pyridoxine.
• Supplementation prevents peripheral neuropathy, a common side effect of INH-induced deficiency.

category: Describe mechanism of action, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: The selective toxicity of Acyclovir is primarily due to its initial phosphorylation by the virus-specified enzyme [___], which is absent in non-infected host cells.
back: Thymidine kinase.

category: Describe mechanism of action, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: A 28-year-old male treated for a UTI with Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole develops jaundice, dark urine, and severe anemia. Identify the underlying biochemical defect triggered by this antibiotic.
back:
• Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency.
• Sulfonamides cause oxidative stress leading to hemolysis in G6PD-deficient individuals.

category: Describe mechanism of action, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Explain how HIV Protease Inhibitors (e.g., Atazanavir) prevent the production of infectious viral particles.
back:
• They inhibit the viral protease enzyme that cleaves the Gag-Pol polyprotein precursor.
• This prevents the processing of viral proteins into functional forms, resulting in immature, noninfectious virions.

category: Describe mechanism of action, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Contrast the effects of Fluoroquinolones and Sulfonamides on bacterial growth classification (Cidal vs. Static) based on their primary targets.
back:
• Fluoroquinolones: Bactericidal; inhibit DNA gyrase/Topoisomerase IV, causing lethal DNA breaks.
• Sulfonamides: Bacteriostatic; inhibit dihydropteroate synthase, arresting folate synthesis and growth without immediate killing.

category: Describe mechanism of action, clinical uses, and adverse effects
front: Name the specific viral enzyme targeted by Oseltamivir to prevent the release of progeny influenza viruses from infected host cells.
back: Neuraminidase.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: The clinical sign characterized by the detachment of the superficial epidermis from the basal layer upon applying lateral pressure is a positive [___].
back:
• Nikolsky sign
  • Indicates widespread epidermal necrosis and loss of cell-cell adhesion (acantholysis).

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: A 25-year-old male recently started on Allopurinol presents with a high-grade fever, sore throat, and 'gritty' eyes, followed by the sudden onset of painful, dusky erythematous macules and mucosal erosions. Identify the most likely diagnosis.
back:
• Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS)
  • Characterized by a flu-like prodrome and severe mucocutaneous involvement.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: Explain the role of CD8+ cytotoxic T-lymphocytes in the pathophysiology of epidermal sloughing in SJS.
back:
• T cells induce widespread keratinocyte apoptosis.
  • Mediated via the release of granulysin, perforin, and granzymes.
  • Fas-Fas ligand interactions further trigger cell death pathways.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: Contrast the clinical classification of Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) versus Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) based on skin detachment criteria.
back:
• SJS: <10% Total Body Surface Area (TBSA) detachment.
  • SJS/TEN Overlap: 10–30% TBSA detachment.
  • TEN: >30% TBSA detachment.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: Identify the minimum diagnostic requirement for mucosal involvement in Stevens-Johnson Syndrome.
back:
• Involvement of at least two distinct mucosal sites.
  • Commonly includes oral (erosions/crusting), conjunctival (purulent discharge), or urogenital surfaces.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: The most frequent pharmacological triggers for SJS in the Pakistani clinical setting are [___], such as Sulfonamides.
back:
• Antibiotics (specifically Sulfonamides)
  • Other triggers include Antiepileptics (Phenytoin, Carbamazepine) and Allopurinol.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: A patient with suspected SJS develops severe photophobia and subconjunctival hemorrhage. Mention the most critical ocular complications to monitor.
back:
• Symblepharon (adhesion of eyelid to eyeball).
  • Corneal scarring and potential blindness.
  • Trichiasis and chronic dry eye syndrome.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: How does the morphology of the 'atypical target lesion' in SJS differ from the 'classic target lesion' seen in Erythema Multiforme?
back:
• SJS atypical targets: Flat, dusky, two-zoned macules with poorly defined borders.
  • EM classic targets: Raised, three-zoned lesions with a 'bull's eye' appearance.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: Distinguish the typical anatomical distribution of SJS lesions from those of Erythema Multiforme (EM).
back:
• SJS: Predominantly affects the trunk and face; spreads symmetrically.
  • EM: Usually acral distribution (hands, feet, and extensor surfaces).

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: Specify the clinical phase that typically precedes the skin eruption in SJS by 1 to 3 days.
back:
• Prodromal phase
  • Presents with non-specific symptoms: High fever, malaise, cough, and rhinitis.

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: Trimethoprim selectively inhibits the bacterial enzyme [___], preventing the conversion of dihydrofolic acid to tetrahydrofolic acid.
back:
● Dihydrofolate reductase
● Leads to inhibition of purine synthesis
● Ultimately halts bacterial DNA production

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
coreConcept: Cotrimoxazole Adverse Electrolyte and Renal Effects
front: An AIDS patient on high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for PCP treatment presents with hyperkalemia and hyponatremia. State the likely cause and clinical significance of their serum creatinine rise.
back:
● Trimethoprim blocks renal amiloride-sensitive sodium channels (causing hyperkalemia)
● Serum creatinine rises due to inhibition of distal tubule secretion
● No actual decrease in glomerular filtration rate (GFR)

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: Explain the biochemical basis for the synergistic, often bactericidal effect of combining trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole.
back:
● Sequential blockade of folic acid synthesis
● Sulfonamide inhibits dihydropteroate synthase
● Trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase
● More complete growth inhibition than monotherapy

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: Contrast the pharmacokinetics of trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole regarding their volume of distribution and the resulting steady-state plasma ratio.
back:
● Trimethoprim: More lipid-soluble, larger volume of distribution
● Ratio: 1:5 (tablet) vs 1:20 (plasma concentration)
● 1:20 ratio is optimal for in vitro synergy

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: Identify the primary mechanism of acquired resistance to trimethoprim in clinical bacterial isolates.
back:
● Plasmid-encoded resistant dihydrofolate reductases
● Overproduction of dihydrofolate reductase
● Reduced cell permeability to the drug

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: Sulfonamides taken near the end of pregnancy should be avoided as they increase the risk of [___] in newborns.
back:
● Kernicterus
● Displace bilirubin from albumin binding sites
● Cross the placenta and enter fetal circulation

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: A patient with a G6PD deficiency develops dark urine and anemia after starting trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for a UTI. What specific drug component is responsible and why?
back:
● Sulfamethoxazole (Sulfonamide component)
● Provokes acute hemolytic reactions in G6PD-deficient patients
● Causes oxidative stress to erythrocytes

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: Describe the specific clinical utility of trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole in treating infections caused by Stenotrophomonas maltophilia.
back:
● Drug of choice for this multidrug-resistant organism
● Requires high doses (15–20 mg/kg/d trimethoprim component)
● Effective against Nocardia and Listeria as well

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: Differentiate the administration requirements for trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole in patients with a creatinine clearance between 15–30 mL/min compared to normal renal function.
back:
● Dose reduction by half is required
● Due to primary renal excretion of both components
● Prevents accumulation and crystalluria

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: List the three primary hematopoietic disturbances caused by the antifolate action of trimethoprim.
back:
● Megaloblastic anemia
● Leukopenia
● Granulocytopenia
● Can be reversed with folinic acid supplementation

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: The bacterial enzyme specifically inhibited by trimethoprim, which prevents the reduction of dihydrofolate to the active form tetrahydrofolate, is [___].
back: • Dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) • This block prevents the synthesis of purines and ultimately bacterial DNA.

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: A 32-year-old patient with AIDS presents with a non-productive cough, fever, and diffuse interstitial infiltrates on chest X-ray. Sputum silver stain identifies Pneumocystis jiroveci. Identify the first-line pharmacotherapy.
back: • High-dose Co-trimoxazole (Trimethoprim-Sulfamethoxazole) • Standard 21-day course • Inhibits folate synthesis required for the pathogen's nucleic acid production.

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: Explain the biological mechanism of 'sequential blockade' achieved by the combination of trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole.
back: • Sulfamethoxazole inhibits dihydropteroate synthase (step 1) • Trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (step 2) • This double blockade results in bactericidal synergy.

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: A patient fails to respond to Co-trimoxazole therapy. If resistance is plasmid-mediated, contrast the biochemical changes seen in the targets of Sulfamethoxazole versus Trimethoprim.
back: • Sulfonamide resistance: Production of dihydropteroate synthase with low drug affinity or increased PABA production • Trimethoprim resistance: Production of dihydrofolate reductase with reduced drug binding affinity.

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: Identify the primary route of elimination for Co-trimoxazole and the necessary dosage modification in patients with a creatinine clearance below 30 mL/min.
back: • Renal excretion (glomerular filtration and tubular secretion) • Requires a 50% dose reduction to avoid accumulation and toxicity.

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: The administration of sulfonamides to neonates or near-term pregnant women is contraindicated because it displaces bilirubin from albumin, potentially causing [___].
back: • Kernicterus (bilirubin-induced encephalopathy) • Free bilirubin crosses the blood-brain barrier in the neonate, leading to neurological damage.

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: A patient with AIDS being treated for pneumonia develops hyperkalemia and a rise in serum creatinine, though BUN remains stable. Explain the pharmacological cause of these laboratory findings.
back: • Trimethoprim inhibits epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) in the distal tubule (hyperkalemia) • Trimethoprim competes with creatinine for renal tubular secretion (spurious creatinine rise).

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: Explain why trimethoprim achieves significantly higher concentrations in the prostate and vaginal fluids compared to plasma.
back: • Ion trapping mechanism • Trimethoprim is a weak base that becomes ionized and trapped in the relatively acidic environment of the prostate and vagina.

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: Contrast the metabolic pathway step inhibited by sulfonamides versus the step inhibited by trimethoprim in bacterial folate synthesis.
back: • Sulfonamides: Compete with PABA to inhibit dihydropteroate synthase • Trimethoprim: Competitively inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR).

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: List three clinically significant organisms, besides common Gram-negatives, that are typically susceptible to Co-trimoxazole.
back: • Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) • Nocardia species • Toxoplasma gondii

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: In Stevens-Johnson Syndrome, clinically significant mucosal necrosis must be present at a minimum of [___] different anatomical sites for a classic diagnosis.
back: Two. Most commonly, these include the oral cavity and the conjunctiva, though urogenital involvement is also a frequent clinical hallmark.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: A 30-year-old male presents with a high-grade fever, painful swallowing, and dusky erythematous macules on his trunk one week after starting a sulfonamide. Examination reveals hemorrhagic crusting of the lips. Identify the most likely diagnosis.
back: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS). The vermilion border hemorrhagic crusting is pathognomonic for drug-induced mucosal involvement.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: Explain the role of keratinocyte apoptosis in the progression of cutaneous SJS lesions from macules to bullae.
back: Widespread apoptosis causes full-thickness epidermal necrosis. This leads to the separation of the epidermis from the dermis, manifesting clinically as flaccid bullae and sheets of denuded skin.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: Contrast the typical triggers and mucosal extent of Erythema Multiforme (EM) Major with Stevens-Johnson Syndrome.
back: Triggers: EM Major is usually post-viral (HSV); SJS is usually drug-induced. Extent: EM Major has limited oral involvement; SJS involves extensive necrosis of multiple mucosal surfaces.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: Identify the characteristic systemic prodromal symptoms that typically precede the cutaneous eruptions of Stevens-Johnson Syndrome.
back: Flu-like symptoms. These include fever, malaise, myalgia, and sore throat, occurring one to three days before lesions appear.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: The clinical sign elicited by applying lateral pressure to the skin, causing epidermal separation from the dermis in SJS, is the [___] sign.
back: Nikolsky Sign. A positive result indicates a loss of skin cohesion due to widespread epidermal necrolysis.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: A patient with SJS develops severe conjunctival purulence and pseudomembranes. If left untreated, describe the most likely chronic ocular complication.
back: Symblepharon. This is the adhesion of the palpebral conjunctiva to the bulbar conjunctiva, potentially leading to blindness.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: Differentiate the depth of epidermal cleavage in SJS from that seen in Staphylococcal Scalded Skin Syndrome (SSSS).
back: SJS cleavage occurs at the dermo-epidermal junction (full-thickness necrosis). SSSS cleavage is superficial, occurring at the granular layer, and consistently spares the mucosa.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: Contrast Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) regarding the extent of body surface area (BSA) detachment.
back: SJS: Involves <10% BSA detachment. TEN: Involves >30% BSA detachment. The 10-30% range is classified as SJS-TEN overlap.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: Identify the specific visceral clinical finding that signifies respiratory tract mucosal involvement in severe SJS cases.
back: Bronchial epithelial sloughing. This manifests clinically as cough, dyspnea, and hypoxemia, often requiring mechanical ventilation.

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: Trimethoprim achieves its antibacterial effect by selectively inhibiting the enzyme [___], which prevents the conversion of dihydrofolic acid to tetrahydrofolic acid.
back:
• Dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR)
• This blocks the synthesis of purines and ultimately DNA
• Trimethoprim is a much more efficient inhibitor of the bacterial enzyme than the mammalian version.

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: A 35-year-old AIDS patient with a CD4 count of 150 cells/μL is prescribed daily double-strength co-trimoxazole. This is the first-line prophylactic agent to prevent pneumonia caused by [___].
back:
• Pneumocystis jiroveci (formerly P. carinii)
• It also provides secondary prophylaxis against Toxoplasma gondii
• High doses (15–20 mg/kg/d of TMP) are required for active treatment.

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: Explain the role of 'sequential blockade' in the synergy between Sulfamethoxazole and Trimethoprim.
back:
• Sulfamethoxazole inhibits dihydropteroate synthase (competes with PABA)
• Trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase
• This two-step inhibition in the same metabolic pathway results in bactericidal activity.

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: Contrast the mechanism of trimethoprim-induced creatinine elevation with sulfonamide-induced renal toxicity.
back:
• Trimethoprim: Inhibits renal tubular secretion of creatinine (false elevation; GFR is unchanged)
• Sulfonamides: Can cause true toxicity via crystalluria (precipitation in acidic urine) or allergic interstitial nephritis.

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: State the standard pharmacokinetic ratio of Trimethoprim to Sulfamethoxazole achieved in the plasma after oral dosing.
back:
• 1:20 (Trimethoprim to Sulfamethoxazole)
• Note: The formulation ratio in the tablet is 1:5 (e.g., 160mg TMP to 800mg SMZ)
• The 1:20 plasma ratio is optimal for synergistic antimicrobial activity.

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole can cause [___] as a common electrolyte disturbance, especially in elderly patients or those with renal impairment.
back:
• Hyperkalemia
• It can also cause hyponatremia, particularly in patients with AIDS
• Monitoring is essential when combined with other potassium-sparing drugs.

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: A patient with a history of G6PD deficiency is treated with Co-trimoxazole for a UTI. Describe the primary hematological risk for this patient.
back:
• Acute Hemolytic Anemia
• Other hematological toxicities include megaloblastic anemia, leukopenia, and granulocytopenia
• These are predictable effects of antifolate drugs.

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: Describe the most significant plasmid-encoded mechanism of bacterial resistance to Trimethoprim.
back:
• Production of altered dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR)
• The resistant enzyme has a significantly reduced affinity for the drug
• Can also be due to reduced cell permeability or DHFR overproduction.

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: Contrast the activity of Co-trimoxazole (TMP-SMZ) against Staphylococcus aureus versus Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
back:
• S. aureus: Highly active against both MSSA and MRSA (community-acquired strains)
• P. aeruginosa: Intrinsically resistant to Co-trimoxazole
• It is also inactive against Mycoplasma pneumoniae.

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: Identify the primary route of elimination for Trimethoprim and the threshold for dose reduction.
back:
• Renal Excretion (30–60% excreted in urine within 24 hours)
• Dose should be reduced by half if Creatinine Clearance is 15–30 mL/min
• It concentrates well in acidic prostatic and vaginal fluids.

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: Trimethoprim selectively inhibits the bacterial enzyme [___], which prevents the conversion of dihydrofolic acid to its active form, tetrahydrofolic acid.
back:
• Dihydrofolate reductase
• This step is critical for purine synthesis and subsequent DNA production.

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: An AIDS patient treated with high-dose Cotrimoxazole develops megaloblastic anemia and leukopenia. This is caused by the drug's antagonism of [___] in the host.
back:
• Folate (Folic acid)
• Although trimethoprim is more selective for bacterial enzymes, high doses can affect human dihydrofolate reductase.

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: Explain the pharmacodynamic rationale for the synergistic 'sequential blockade' seen in Cotrimoxazole (TMP-SMZ).
back:
• Sulfamethoxazole inhibits dihydropteroate synthase (competes with PABA).
• Trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase.
• Blocking two consecutive steps in folate synthesis provides bactericidal activity.

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: A patient with severe Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia fails to respond to Cotrimoxazole. Contrast the mechanism of the primary alternative agent, Pentamidine, with TMP-SMZ.
back:
• TMP-SMZ: Inhibits folate/DNA synthesis pathway.
• Pentamidine: Interferes with protozoal DNA/RNA/protein synthesis and energy metabolism (exact mechanism uncertain).

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: Why does Trimethoprim achieve higher concentrations in prostatic and vaginal fluids compared to plasma?
back:
• It is a weak base.
• It becomes ion-trapped and concentrated in these fluids because they are more acidic than plasma.

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: The most common mechanism of acquired bacterial resistance to trimethoprim is the production of [___].
back:
• Altered dihydrofolate reductase enzymes
• These are often plasmid-encoded and have a significantly lower affinity for the drug.

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: A patient on maintenance therapy for recurrent UTIs presents with a serum potassium of 5.6 mEq/L. Explain the likely pharmacological cause involving their antibiotic.
back:
• Trimethoprim component
• It blocks amiloride-sensitive sodium channels in the distal nephron, inhibiting potassium secretion similar to potassium-sparing diuretics.

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: Explain how Trimethoprim causes a rise in serum creatinine without affecting the true Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR).
back:
• Trimethoprim competitively inhibits the active tubular secretion of creatinine.
• This elevates serum creatinine levels while the actual filtration capacity (GFR) remains unchanged.

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: Contrast the specific substrates targeted by Sulfamethoxazole versus Trimethoprim in the folate metabolic loop.
back:
• Sulfamethoxazole: Competes with p-aminobenzoic acid (PABA) for dihydropteroate synthase.
• Trimethoprim: Competes with dihydrofolic acid for dihydrofolate reductase.

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: Identify the primary clinical indication for high-dose (15-20 mg/kg) intravenous Cotrimoxazole.
back:
• Severe Pneumocystis jiroveci pneumonia (PCP)
• It is the first-line treatment for both HIV-associated and non-HIV-associated PCP.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: Stevens-Johnson Syndrome is a life-threatening mucocutaneous reaction characterized by detachment of the epidermis and extensive erosions of the [___].
back: - Mucous membranes; Clinical features include painful erosions in the mouth, eyes, and genitalia; Often presents as a severe, potentially fatal eruption secondary to drug hypersensitivity.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: A patient on atazanavir therapy develops painful oral ulcers and atypical target lesions on <10% of her body. Identify the underlying hypersensitivity condition and its expected clinical severity.
back: - Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS); Characterized by fever and <10% epidermal detachment; NNRTIs like Nevirapine have a higher reported incidence compared to other antiretroviral classes.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: Explain the characteristic progression of skin and mucosal lesions during the acute phase of Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS).
back: - Prodromal fever and malaise occur first; Rapid onset of painful erythematous macules follows; Progresses to vesicle formation, bullae, and extensive sloughing of skin and mucosal surfaces.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: A patient presents with widespread skin sloughing. Differentiate between a diagnosis of Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) and Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN) based on the total body surface area (BSA) involved.
back: - SJS is limited to <10% body surface area (BSA) epidermal detachment; TEN is more severe, involving >30% BSA detachment; Clinical presentation of mucosal involvement is identical in both conditions.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: Identify the specific drug classes that pharmacologically increase the risk of Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS) according to the provided infectious disease text.
back: - Sulfonamides (e.g., sulfamethoxazole); Non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs like nevirapine); Protease inhibitors (PIs like atazanavir); Thiabendazole is also associated with rare, fatal cases.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: A hallmark diagnostic finding in Stevens-Johnson Syndrome is the involvement of at least [___] or more distinct mucous membrane sites.
back: - Two (2); Oral, ocular, and urogenital membranes are most frequently affected; Involvement is usually accompanied by painful hemorrhagic crusting and severe inflammation.

category: Outline clinical features of Steven Johnsons Syndrome
front: A patient develops extensive blistering and mucosal sloughing after starting Thiabendazole. Apply your knowledge of rare thiabendazole toxicities to identify this life-threatening syndrome.
back: - Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS); This condition is a rare but documented life-threatening complication of thiabendazole therapy; Clinical management requires immediate drug withdrawal and intensive supportive management.

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: Trimethoprim achieves its antibacterial effect by selectively inhibiting the enzyme [___], which prevents the conversion of dihydrofolic acid to tetrahydrofolic acid.
back:
• Dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR)
• Prevents synthesis of purines
• Ultimately halts DNA production and bacterial replication

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: A patient with AIDS being treated for Pneumocystis pneumonia develops a severe bullous skin eruption and mucosal erosions. Identify this life-threatening hypersensitivity reaction and the specific drug component usually responsible.
back:
• Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS)
• Sulfamethoxazole component
• Can progress to Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis (TEN)

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: Explain the biochemical basis for the synergistic 'sequential blockade' achieved by the combination of Sulfamethoxazole and Trimethoprim.
back:
• Sulfamethoxazole inhibits dihydropteroate synthase (Step 1)
• Trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (Step 2)
• Blocks two consecutive steps in the microbial folic acid pathway

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: Contrast the formulation ratio of Sulfamethoxazole to Trimethoprim in a 'Double Strength' (DS) tablet with the resulting peak steady-state plasma ratio in a patient with normal renal function.
back:
• Formulation ratio: 5:1 (800mg to 160mg)
• Plasma ratio: 20:1
• Difference driven by Trimethoprim's larger volume of distribution and higher lipid solubility

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: By what specific renal mechanism does Trimethoprim cause a mild rise in serum creatinine without actually decreasing the glomerular filtration rate (GFR)?
back:
• Inhibition of renal tubular secretion of creatinine
• Occurs at the distal tubule
• Does not reflect true renal injury or impaired filtration

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: Trimethoprim can cause a reversible clinical elevation in serum [___] because it inhibits the renal epithelial sodium channels in the distal tubule, chemically acting like the diuretic amiloride.
back:
• Potassium (Hyperkalemia)
• Blocks Na+/K+ exchange
• Risk increases in elderly, renal patients, or those on ACE inhibitors

category: Explain mechanism of actions, resistance, antibacterial spectrum, pharmacokinetics, clinical uses and adverse effects of trimethoprim andcotrimoxazole
front: An HIV-positive patient presents with a CD4 count <200/μL and a non-productive cough. If Co-trimoxazole is initiated, identify the target organism and its clinical indication in this context.
back:
• Pneumocystis jirovecii
• Prophylaxis and treatment of Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP)
• Standard of care for immunocompromised hosts

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Aminoglycosides are bactericidal inhibitors of protein synthesis that consist of amino sugars linked via glycosidic bonds to a hexose ring, which is either streptidine or [___].
back:
• 2-deoxystreptamine.
• This hexose ring structure differentiates various members of the class (e.g., Streptomycin has streptidine, while Gentamicin has 2-deoxystreptamine).

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: A 45-year-old male is scheduled for elective colorectal surgery. He is prescribed a non-absorbable oral aminoglycoside to reduce aerobic bowel flora. Identify the drug and its primary classification based on use.
back:
• Neomycin.
• Classified as a non-absorbable aminoglycoside.
• Used orally for bowel preparation (with erythromycin) or hepatic encephalopathy; restricted from systemic use due to high toxicity.

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Explain the physiological requirement for aminoglycoside transport across the bacterial cytoplasmic membrane and how this limits their antimicrobial spectrum.
back:
• Requires an oxygen-dependent active transport process coupled to a proton pump.
• Clinical implication: This limits the spectrum strictly to aerobic bacteria; all anaerobes are intrinsically resistant.

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Contrast Gentamicin and Amikacin regarding their susceptibility to bacterial modifying enzymes and their clinical role in resistant infections.
back:
• Gentamicin: Easily inactivated by plasmid-encoded transferase enzymes (adenylylation, phosphorylation, etc.).
• Amikacin: Semisynthetic derivative protected from most enzymes.
• Clinical Role: Amikacin has the broadest spectrum, reserved for infections resistant to other aminoglycosides.

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Classify Streptomycin based on its primary therapeutic indications in modern clinical practice.
back:
• Second-line agent for Tuberculosis (in combination).
• First-line/Drug of Choice for Plague (Yersinia pestis) and Tularemia.
• Adjunct for Streptococcal or Enterococcal endocarditis.

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: [___] is an aminocyclitol antibiotic structurally related to aminoglycosides that is used almost solely as an alternative for drug-resistant gonorrhea in penicillin-allergic patients.
back:
• Spectinomycin.
• Lacks amino sugars and glycosidic bonds found in true aminoglycosides.
• Notable for lacking cross-resistance with other anti-gonorrhea drugs.

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: A 12-year-old patient with cystic fibrosis presents with a lower respiratory tract infection caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Which aminoglycoside is specifically formulated for inhalation in this setting?
back:
• Tobramycin.
• Administered as a 300 mg aerosolized dose.
• High local concentrations improve efficacy while minimizing systemic toxicities (ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity).

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Describe how aminoglycosides carry out their bactericidal effect through their interactions with the 30S ribosomal subunit.
back:
• Blocks formation of the initiation complex.
• Induces mRNA misreading, creating nonfunctional proteins.
• Breaks up polysomes into monosomes.
• Unique for being bactericidal despite being protein synthesis inhibitors.

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Contrast once-daily aminoglycoside dosing with conventional multiple-daily dosing regarding efficacy and toxicity risk.
back:
• Once-daily: Exploits concentration-dependent killing and Post-Antibiotic Effect (PAE).
• Toxicity: Lower risk because the 'washout' period reduces cumulative accumulation in the renal cortex.

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Classify Neomycin, Amikacin, and Streptomycin according to their predominant type of eighth cranial nerve toxicity.
back:
• Auditory (Hearing Loss): Neomycin, Amikacin, Kanamycin.
• Vestibular (Vertigo/Ataxia): Streptomycin, Gentamicin.
• Tobramycin affects both systems equally.

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: The primary structural classification of aminoglycosides is based on the [___] hexose ring which serves as the scaffold for glycosidically linked amino sugars.
back:
- Aminocyclitol
- Includes Streptidine (in Streptomycin)
- Includes 2-Deoxystreptamine (in Gentamicin, Amikacin, and Tobramycin)

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: A 40-year-old male is undergoing elective bowel surgery. Identify the specific classification of aminoglycosides used for 'bowel preparation' and provide a drug example.
back:
- Non-absorbable Aminoglycosides
- Example: Neomycin (or Kanamycin)
- Used orally to suppress aerobic flora locally before surgery

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Explain the role of the 2-deoxystreptamine ring in the classification and function of most systemic aminoglycosides.
back:
- Acts as the central hexose ring
- Allows binding to the 30S ribosomal subunit
- Found in Gentamicin, Tobramycin, and Amikacin (but not Streptomycin)

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Contrast the structural origins and resistance profiles of Amikacin versus its parent compound, Kanamycin.
back:
- Amikacin: Semisynthetic derivative
- Kanamycin: Natural product
- Amikacin is resistant to most aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes that inactivate Kanamycin

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Identify the metabolic requirement for the active transport of aminoglycosides into bacterial cells, effectively excluding anaerobes from their spectrum.
back:
- Oxygen-dependent active transport
- Requires a transmembrane electrochemical gradient
- Inactive in anaerobic or low-pH environments

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: [___] is a recently developed aminoglycoside derived from sisomicin that is classified by its ability to resist almost all aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes.
back:
- Plazomicin
- Used for carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae
- Structurally unsaturated in Ring I compared to Amikacin

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: A patient with multi-drug resistant tuberculosis requires an injectable agent. Identify the natural aminoglycoside that contains a Streptidine ring instead of a 2-Deoxystreptamine ring.
back:
- Streptomycin
- Second-line agent for M. tuberculosis
- Isolated from Streptomyces griseus

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Explain how the ethyl group modification at the 1-amino position classifies Netilmicin as a distinct agent from Gentamicin.
back:
- Sterically protects the molecule from enzymatic degradation
- Specifically targets the 3-amino and 2-hydroxyl positions
- Effective against some gentamicin-resistant strains

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Contrast the clinical classification of Tobramycin and Gentamicin regarding their potency against Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
back:
- Tobramycin: More potent against P. aeruginosa
- Gentamicin: Slightly more active against Serratia marcescens
- Both are systemic bactericidal inhibitors of protein synthesis

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Identify the aminocyclitol drug that is structurally related to aminoglycosides but lacks amino sugars and glycosidic bonds, used primarily for gonorrhea.
back:
- Spectinomycin
- Alternative for drug-resistant gonorrhea
- Lacks the typical side effects of traditional aminoglycosides

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Aminoglycosides are classified by their central hexose ring; streptomycin is unique in containing a [___] ring, while most other clinical agents contain 2-deoxystreptamine.
back:
• Streptidine
• All others (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) utilize a 2-deoxystreptamine nucleus.

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: A 45-year-old burn patient develops sepsis due to Pseudomonas aeruginosa. A combination regimen including tobramycin is started. Explain the pharmacodynamic rationale for once-daily dosing in this patient.
back:
• Concentration-dependent killing: Higher peaks increase the rate/extent of bacterial death.
• Postantibiotic effect (PAE): Activity persists hours after blood levels drop.
• Toxicity reduction: Minimizes time above the threshold for ear/kidney damage.

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Explain the mechanism by which cell wall-active agents (e.g. penicillins) enhance the bactericidal activity of aminoglycosides specifically in treating Enterococcal infections.
back:
• Synergism: β-lactams disrupt cell wall integrity, facilitating drug entry into the cytoplasm.
• Enhances uptake: Overcomes the natural permeability barrier that renders enterococci relatively resistant to monotherapy.

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Contrast the clinical ototoxicity patterns typically observed with streptomycin/gentamicin versus those seen with amikacin/kanamycin.
back:
• Streptomycin/Gentamicin: Primarily vestibulotoxic, causing vertigo, ataxia, and loss of balance.
• Amikacin/Kanamycin: Primarily auditory toxic, resulting in tinnitus and high-frequency hearing loss.

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Explain why spectinomycin is classified as an aminocyclitol rather than a true aminoglycoside despite being used for similar indications.
back:
• Structural difference: It lacks both amino sugars and glycosidic bonds.
• Clinical use: Reserved almost exclusively for drug-resistant or penicillin-allergic gonorrhea.

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Aminoglycosides are classified as bactericidal inhibitors of protein synthesis that bind irreversibly to the [___] ribosomal subunit.
back:
• 30S ribosomal subunit
• Mechanisms include interference with the initiation complex, misreading of mRNA, and polysome breakup into nonfunctional monosomes.

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: A patient with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis requires an injectable agent. Identify the specific aminoglycoside that is a semisynthetic derivative of kanamycin and generally resists inactivation by many modifying enzymes.
back:
• Amikacin
• Indicated for streptomycin-resistant strains or multidrug-resistant M. tuberculosis; requires serum concentration monitoring.

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: A patient fails therapy for a carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter infection. Explain the biochemical rationale for using the newly developed synthetic aminoglycoside Plazomicin over older agents.
back:
• Enzyme resistance: Modified to resist most adenylylation, acetylation, and phosphorylation transferases.
• Parent structure: Synthetic molecule derived from sisomicin with 2-4 fold lower MICs against nonfermenters.

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Contrast the therapeutic niches of the systemic aminoglycosides (e.g. gentamicin) with the non-systemic group (e.g. neomycin/paromomycin).
back:
• Systemic: Well-absorbed parenterally for sepsis and endocarditis; too toxic for routine oral use.
• Non-systemic: Poorly absorbed; limited to topical skin infections, preoperative bowel preparation, or hepatic encephalopathy.

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Identify the specific aminoglycoside derived from Micromonospora purpurea that exists as a clinical mixture of three constituents: C1, C1A, and C2.
back:
• Gentamicin
• Most commonly used aminoglycoside for severe Gram-negative infections and synergistic treatment of Gram-positive endocarditis.

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Aminoglycosides are classified as bactericidal protein synthesis inhibitors because they irreversibly bind to the [___] subunit of the bacterial ribosome.
back:
*   30S ribosomal subunit
*   Blocks initiation complex formation
*   Causes misreading of mRNA and polysome disruption.

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: A patient requires an aminoglycoside with the broadest spectrum of activity, specifically categorized as a semisynthetic derivative of Kanamycin that resists most aminoglycoside-inactivating enzymes. Identify the drug: [___].
back:
*   Amikacin
*   Resistant to many enzymes that inactivate gentamicin and tobramycin
*   Often used for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis.

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Explain the pharmacodynamic classification of aminoglycosides regarding their killing action and the clinical significance of their postantibiotic effect (PAE).
back:
*   Concentration-dependent killing: Higher peak levels increase killing rate
*   Significant PAE: Activity persists after drug falls below MIC
*   Basis for once-daily dosing regimens.

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Contrast the clinical classification of 'Systemic' versus 'Topical/Luminal' aminoglycosides, providing a representative agent for each and its primary toxicity limitation.
back:
*   Systemic: Gentamicin/Tobramycin; limited by ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity
*   Topical/Luminal: Neomycin/Paromomycin; limited by extreme systemic toxicity if absorbed.

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Classify the natural aminoglycosides according to their biological source, distinguishing between those derived from Streptomyces and those from Micromonospora.
back:
*   Streptomyces: Streptomycin, Tobramycin, Kanamycin, Neomycin
*   Micromonospora: Gentamicin, Sisomicin, Netilmicin (semisynthetic from Sisomicin).

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: [___] is a specific aminoglycoside classified as a luminal agent because it is not significantly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract, making it the drug of choice for intestinal amebiasis.
back:
*   Paromomycin
*   Oral aminoglycoside with minimal systemic bioavailability
*   Acts directly on trophozoites in the gut lumen.

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: A 25-year-old male with a severe penicillin allergy requires treatment for drug-resistant gonorrhea. The alternative agent from the aminocyclitol class that lacks amino sugars and glycosidic bonds is [___].
back:
*   Spectinomycin
*   Structurally related to aminoglycosides but distinct subclass
*   Used solely for gonorrhea in penicillin-allergic or resistant cases.

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Aminoglycosides are chemically categorized by their central hexose ring, which is [___] in streptomycin and 2-deoxystreptamine in most other clinical members.
back:
*   Streptidine
*   Linked to amino sugars via glycosidic bonds
*   Determines chemical subclass within the family

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: A patient with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis requires an injectable agent that is less toxic than kanamycin. The appropriate semisynthetic derivative to initiate is [___].
back:
*   Amikacin
*   Derivative of kanamycin
*   Superior resistance to aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Explain the biological basis for the suffix classification of 'Gentamicin' (-micin) versus 'Streptomycin' (-mycin).
back:
*   -mycin: Derived from the genus Streptomyces
*   -micin: Derived from the genus Micromonospora
*   Classified by their original fungal-like bacterial sources

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: A patient with a superficial infected burn receives a topical ointment, while a patient with Serratia sepsis receives an IV infusion. Contrast these two aminoglycoside classifications regarding identity and route restriction.
back:
*   Topical: Neomycin (restricted due to extreme systemic toxicity)
*   Systemic (IV): Gentamicin or Tobramycin
*   Classification is based on the therapeutic index and risk of nephrotoxicity

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Name the synthetic aminoglycoside derived from sisomicin that is uniquely effective against most carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae.
back:
*   Plazomicin
*   Derivative of sisomicin
*   Specifically designed to resist inactivation by aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Aminoglycosides are notably ineffective against [___] bacteria because their entry into the cell is an oxygen-dependent process requiring an electrochemical gradient.
back:
*   Anaerobic
*   Ineffective in low pH or anaerobic environments
*   Uptake is coupled to a proton pump

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: A patient presents with Pseudomonas aeruginosa sepsis. While gentamicin is an option, which specific aminoglycoside is classified as having slightly superior potency against this pathogen?
back:
*   Tobramycin
*   Similar pharmacology to gentamicin
*   Indicated preferentially for serious Pseudomonas infections

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: A laboratory isolate of Klebsiella is resistant to gentamicin. Explain the structural modification that allows the semisynthetic derivative Netilmicin to potentially remain active.
back:
*   1-N-ethyl group on the 2-deoxystreptamine ring
*   Provides steric protection against degradation
*   Resists enzymes targeting 3-amino and 2-hydroxyl positions

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Contrast the primary hexose nuclei used to divide the chemical structure of aminoglycosides.
back:
*   Streptidine: Unique to Streptomycin
*   2-Deoxystreptamine: Found in Kanamycin, Gentamicin, and Tobramycin
*   Determines chemical classification and receptor binding sites

category: Classify aminoglycosides
front: Which aminoglycoside is classified as a luminal amebicide because it is not significantly absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract?
back:
*   Paromomycin
*   Not used for systemic bacterial disease
*   Eradicates intestinal Entamoeba histolytica

category: Describe the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides
front: Aminoglycosides exert their primary bactericidal effect by irreversibly binding to the [___] subunit of the bacterial ribosome.
back:
• 30S ribosomal subunit.
• This binding blocks the initiation of protein synthesis.
• It also induces mRNA misreading and breaks up polysomes into monosomes.

category: Describe the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides
front: A patient with an anaerobic pelvic abscess fails to respond to Gentamicin therapy. This lack of efficacy is due to the parasite's inability to perform [___] across the cytoplasmic membrane.
back:
• Oxygen-dependent active transport.
• Aminoglycosides require a proton pump and an electrochemical gradient to enter the cytoplasm.
• Anaerobic conditions inhibit this transport, conferring intrinsic resistance.

category: Describe the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides
front: Describe the three distinct ways aminoglycosides interfere with bacterial protein synthesis once they have bound to their ribosomal target.
back:
• Interference with the initiation complex of peptide formation.
• Misreading of mRNA (incorporating incorrect amino acids).
• Breakup of polysomes into nonfunctional monosomes.

category: Describe the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides
front: Contrast the killing dynamics of aminoglycosides with those of Beta-lactam antibiotics regarding concentration versus time dependence.
back:
• Aminoglycosides: Concentration-dependent killing (efficacy increases with higher peak levels).
• Beta-lactams: Time-dependent killing (efficacy depends on duration above MIC).
• Aminoglycosides also possess a significant Post-Antibiotic Effect (PAE).

category: Describe the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides
front: Explain the pharmacodynamic rationale for combining a cell wall-active agent (like Penicillin) with an aminoglycoside for serious infections.
back:
• Synergistic uptake enhancement.
• Cell wall inhibitors (Penicillins/Vancomycin) increase bacterial membrane permeability.
• This facilitates greater entry of the aminoglycoside to its intracellular target.

category: Describe the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides
front: The initial event in the entry of aminoglycosides into Gram-negative bacteria involves passive diffusion via [___] in the outer membrane.
back:
• Porin channels.
• This is followed by active transport across the inner cytoplasmic membrane.
• Transport is coupled to a proton pump using an electrochemical gradient.

category: Describe the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides
front: A hospital isolate of *Serratia marcescens* shows resistance to Gentamicin. The most common biochemical mechanism for acquired resistance in this clinical setting is [___].
back:
• Production of transferase (modifying) enzymes.
• These enzymes inactivate the drug via adenylylation, acetylation, or phosphorylation.
• This prevents the drug from binding to the 30S ribosome.

category: Describe the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides
front: How does the aminoglycoside-induced mechanism of 'mRNA misreading' specifically lead to a bactericidal rather than bacteriostatic effect?
back:
• Incorporation of incorrect amino acids leads to nonfunctional proteins.
• These abnormal proteins may insert into the cell membrane.
• This causes altered permeability, leakage, and eventual cell death.

category: Describe the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides
front: Contrast the activity of aminoglycosides in an acidic environment (e.g., an abscess) compared to an alkaline environment.
back:
• Aminoglycosides are more active at alkaline pH.
• Low extracellular pH reduces the electrochemical gradient.
• This inhibits the active transport needed for the drug to enter the cell.

category: Describe the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides
front: Identify the phenomenon where bacterial growth remains suppressed even after aminoglycoside serum levels fall below the MIC.
back:
• Post-Antibiotic Effect (PAE).
• This allows for effective once-daily (extended-interval) dosing.
• It reduces toxicity while maintaining high bactericidal efficacy.

category: Describe the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides
front: Aminoglycosides cross the bacterial cytoplasmic (inner) membrane via an [___]-dependent active transport process.
back:
• Oxygen-dependent transport.
• Linked to a transmembrane electrochemical gradient (proton pump).
• Inhibited by anaerobic conditions and low extracellular pH.

category: Describe the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides
front: A patient with Pseudomonas sepsis fails to improve on Gentamicin. Analysis reveals a plasmid-encoded enzyme that attaches a phosphate group to the antibiotic. This resistance mechanism is known as [___].
back:
• Enzymatic inactivation by transferases.
• Specifically phosphorylation (also acetylation or adenylylation).
• Most common clinical mechanism of aminoglycoside resistance.

category: Describe the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides
front: Explain the specific impact of aminoglycoside binding on mRNA translation during the elongation phase.
back:
• Causes misreading of the mRNA genetic code.
• Results in the incorporation of incorrect amino acids.
• Leads to the production of nonfunctional, toxic proteins.

category: Describe the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides
front: Contrast the killing dynamics of aminoglycosides with the killing dynamics of beta-lactam antibiotics.
back:
• Aminoglycosides: Concentration-dependent killing (higher peaks increase rate and extent of kill).
• Beta-lactams: Time-dependent killing (efficacy depends on time above the MIC).

category: Describe the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides
front: Identify the three primary ways aminoglycosides interfere with bacterial protein synthesis at the ribosome.
back:
• Interference with the initiation complex of peptide formation.
• Misreading of mRNA (premature termination or nonfunctional protein).
• Breakup of polysomes into nonfunctional monosomes.

category: Describe the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides
front: Aminoglycosides are considered bactericidal because their binding to the [___] ribosomal subunit is irreversible.
back:
• 30S ribosomal subunit.
• Most other protein synthesis inhibitors (e.g., tetracyclines) are reversible and bacteriostatic.

category: Describe the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides
front: A clinician prescribes Penicillin and Gentamicin for a patient with Enterococcal endocarditis. Describe the cellular basis for the synergy between these two agents.
back:
• Penicillin inhibits cell wall synthesis.
• This increases the permeability of the bacterial membrane.
• Results in enhanced aminoglycoside entry into the cytoplasm.

category: Describe the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides
front: How does the 'Post-Antibiotic Effect' (PAE) justify the use of once-daily dosing in aminoglycoside therapy?
back:
• PAE is the persistent suppression of growth after drug levels drop below MIC.
• Allows bactericidal activity to continue during the trough period.
• Maximizes efficacy while minimizing time-dependent toxicities.

category: Describe the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides
front: Contrast the mechanisms of resistance involving the 30S subunit between Streptomycin and Tetracyclines.
back:
• Streptomycin: Mutation or deletion of the specific receptor protein on the 30S subunit.
• Tetracyclines: Production of 'ribosomal protection proteins' that displace the drug.

category: Describe the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides
front: Describe the formation of 'monosomes' induced by aminoglycoside treatment.
back:
• Blockade of translation occurs after one initiation complex forms.
• Polysomes (multiple ribosomes on mRNA) break up.
• Only a single, non-functional ribosome remains on the mRNA strand.

category: Describe the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides
front: Aminoglycosides exert their bactericidal effect by binding irreversibly to the [___] subunit of the bacterial ribosome.
back:
• The 30S ribosomal subunit
• Binding disrupts protein synthesis by causing mRNA misreading and inhibiting the formation of the initiation complex.

category: Describe the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides
front: A patient with a severe Pseudomonas infection is treated with an antibiotic that causes mRNA misreading and synthesis of nonfunctional proteins. Explain why this drug class is ineffective in an anaerobic abscess environment.
back:
• Requires oxygen-dependent active transport to cross the inner membrane
• Transport is coupled to a proton pump/electrochemical gradient
• Anaerobic conditions or low pH reduce this gradient, preventing drug entry.

category: Describe the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides
front: Describe the three distinct ways by which aminoglycosides inhibit bacterial protein synthesis upon binding their ribosomal target.
back:
• Interference with the initiation complex of peptide formation
• Misreading of mRNA, leading to the incorporation of incorrect amino acids
• Breakup of polysomes into nonfunctional monosomes.

category: Describe the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides
front: A patient with sepsis receives Gentamicin, while another with a Chlamydial infection receives Doxycycline. Both drugs bind the 30S ribosome; contrast their resulting pharmacological effects on bacterial viability and binding nature.
back:
• Aminoglycosides (Gentamicin): Irreversible binding; Bactericidal effect
• Tetracyclines (Doxycycline): Reversible binding; Bacteriostatic effect
• Aminoglycosides uniquely cause lethal mRNA misreading, unlike the reversible block of tetracyclines.

category: Describe the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides
front: Identify the primary pharmacological step required for an aminoglycoside to reach the bacterial periplasmic space from the extracellular environment.
back:
• Passive diffusion via porin channels
• Occurs across the lipid bilayer of the outer membrane in Gram-negative bacteria
• This is a prerequisite for subsequent active cytoplasmic transport.

category: Describe the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides
front: The uptake of aminoglycosides into the bacterial cytoplasm is an [___]-dependent process, explaining their inherent lack of activity against Obligate Anaerobes.
back:
• Oxygen-dependent
• Requires the transmembrane electrochemical gradient to power the active transport phase
• Environment must be aerobic for the drug to reach its intracellular target.

category: Describe the mechanism of action of aminoglycosides
front: During treatment for Gram-negative septicemia, it is observed that high peak drug concentrations result in a faster rate of bacterial killing. Name this pharmacological property and the associated effect that permits once-daily dosing.
back:
• Concentration-dependent killing: Higher concentrations kill a larger proportion of bacteria faster
• Postantibiotic effect (PAE): Persistent suppression of growth even after serum levels fall below the MIC.

category: Describe the mechanism of resistance of aminoglycosides
front: The most common clinical mechanism of resistance to aminoglycosides involves the production of a [___] enzyme that inactivates the drug through adenylylation, acetylation, or phosphorylation.
back: Transferase enzyme.

category: Describe the mechanism of resistance of aminoglycosides
front: A 45-year-old burn patient with *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* sepsis fails to respond to tobramycin. Laboratory analysis reveals a lack of porin channels in the outer membrane. This represents resistance due to [___].
back: Impaired drug entry.

category: Describe the mechanism of resistance of aminoglycosides
front: Explain why anaerobic bacteria are intrinsically resistant to aminoglycosides based on the drug's intracellular transport requirements.
back: Aminoglycoside transport into the cytoplasm is an oxygen-dependent process. Anaerobic conditions lack the necessary electrochemical gradient and proton pump activity to move the drug across the cell membrane.

category: Describe the mechanism of resistance of aminoglycosides
front: Contrast the mechanism of ribosomal resistance specifically seen with Streptomycin compared to the most common resistance mechanism seen with Gentamicin.
back:
• Streptomycin: Point mutations in the 30S ribosomal subunit receptor protein.
• Gentamicin: Plasmid-encoded aminoglycoside-modifying (transferase) enzymes including adenylylation, phosphorylation, or acetylation.

category: Describe the mechanism of resistance of aminoglycosides
front: List the three specific chemical modifications performed by bacterial transferase enzymes to inactivate aminoglycosides.
back:
• Adenylylation
• Acetylation
• Phosphorylation

category: Describe the mechanism of resistance of aminoglycosides
front: Resistance due to impaired aminoglycoside entry into Gram-negative bacteria often results from a mutation or deletion of a [___] protein involved in transport.
back: Porin protein.

category: Describe the mechanism of resistance of aminoglycosides
front: A patient with *Enterococcus faecium* endocarditis shows no synergy when Gentamicin is added to Penicillin. This lack of synergy is most likely due to the bacteria producing a [___].
back: Bifunctional modifying enzyme (transferase). This enzyme inactivates the aminoglycoside, preventing it from reaching the 30S ribosome even after penicillin increases cell wall permeability.

category: Describe the mechanism of resistance of aminoglycosides
front: Describe how a single-step mutation in the 30S ribosomal subunit leads to high-level resistance against Streptomycin.
back: The mutation deletes or alters the specific receptor protein on the 30S subunit. This prevents the aminoglycoside from binding to its target, rendering the drug unable to inhibit protein synthesis.

category: Describe the mechanism of resistance of aminoglycosides
front: Contrast the metabolic requirements for aminoglycoside uptake between aerobic and anaerobic growth conditions.
back:
• Aerobic: Uses an oxygen-dependent active transport process coupled to an electrochemical gradient.
• Anaerobic: The required gradient/proton pump is non-functional, preventing drug entry into the cytoplasm.

category: Describe the mechanism of resistance of aminoglycosides
front: Identify the primary reason why Amikacin often remains active against Gram-negative bacteria that have developed resistance to Gentamicin or Tobramycin.
back: Amikacin is structurally resistant to many of the aminoglycoside-modifying (transferase) enzymes that commonly inactivate Gentamicin and Tobramycin.

category: Describe the mechanism of resistance of aminoglycosides
front: The most important clinical mechanism of resistance to aminoglycosides involves the production of bacterial [___] enzymes that inactivate the drug.
back:
• Transferase enzymes
• Includes adenylylation, acetylation, and phosphorylation
• These plasmid-encoded enzymes modify the drug molecule, preventing it from binding to the 30S ribosome.

category: Describe the mechanism of resistance of aminoglycosides
front: A patient with a deep-seated abscess fails to respond to gentamicin despite in vitro susceptibility. The anaerobic environment of the abscess contributes to resistance by [___].
back:
• Inhibiting oxygen-dependent active transport
• Aminoglycoside entry requires an electrochemical gradient
• Anaerobic conditions and low pH reduce this gradient, preventing the drug from reaching the cytoplasm.

category: Describe the mechanism of resistance of aminoglycosides
front: Explain the biological process by which bacterial transferase enzymes typically confer high-level resistance to aminoglycosides.
back:
• Bacteria produce plasmid-encoded enzymes (adenylyltransferase, acetyltransferase, phosphotransferase)
• Enzymes catalyze the attachment of groups to the drug molecule
• The modified aminoglycoside lacks affinity for the 30S ribosomal target.

category: Describe the mechanism of resistance of aminoglycosides
coreConcept: Target Site Mutation vs. Drug Modification
front: Contrast the mechanism of "ribosomal resistance" seen with streptomycin versus the "enzymatic resistance" typical of other aminoglycosides.
back:
• Ribosomal: Point mutations in 30S genes (rpsL or rrs) delete the binding site on the ribosome
• Enzymatic: Transferase enzymes modify the drug itself
• Ribosomal resistance is common for streptomycin but rare for others.

category: Describe the mechanism of resistance of aminoglycosides
front: Identify the three specific chemical modifications bacterial transferase enzymes perform to inactivate aminoglycosides.
back:
• Adenylylation
• Acetylation
• Phosphorylation
• These modifications prevent the drug from effectively binding to its ribosomal protein target.

category: Describe the mechanism of resistance of aminoglycosides
front: Resistance to aminoglycosides via impaired penetration can occur due to the mutation or deletion of [___] proteins in the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria.
back:
• Porin proteins
• Porins provide hydrophilic access through the outer membrane
• Absence or downregulation of proper porin channels prevents the drug from entering the periplasmic space.
