back:
• Rifampin is a potent CYP450 inducer (3A4)
• Effect: Dramatically reduces Protease Inhibitor levels
• Rifabutin: Less potent enzyme induction; fewer drug interactions.

category: Describe the characteristic pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetic properties of Rifampin, Isoniazid, Ethambutol and Pyrazinamide
front: How does Ethambutol specifically inhibit the polymerization of the mycobacterial cell wall?
back:
• Inhibits arabinosyl transferases
• Target: embCAB operon
• Result: Blockade of arabinoglycan synthesis, leading to cell wall instability.

category: Describe the characteristic pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetic properties of Rifampin, Isoniazid, Ethambutol and Pyrazinamide
front: Contrast the renal elimination profiles of Isoniazid and Pyrazinamide regarding necessary dosage adjustments in renal failure.
back:
• Isoniazid: Primarily hepatic metabolism; no adjustment needed
• Pyrazinamide: Metabolites are renally cleared
• Clinical: PZA dosage must be reduced/intermittent in renal impairment.

category: Describe the characteristic pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetic properties of Rifampin, Isoniazid, Ethambutol and Pyrazinamide
front: Which specific biochemical abnormality is universally seen in patients taking Pyrazinamide due to competition with renal urate excretion?
back:
• Hyperuricemia
• Mechanism: Inhibits renal excretion of uric acid
• Clinical: Usually asymptomatic but can precipitate gouty arthritis.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: To prevent peripheral neuropathy during isoniazid (INH) therapy, patients should be co-administered [___].
back:
• Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
• INH promotes B6 excretion
• Essential for slow acetylators, alcoholics, or malnourished patients.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: A 45-year-old male on TB therapy reports difficulty distinguishing traffic light colors and blurred vision. The drug most likely responsible is [___].
back:
• Ethambutol
• Causes dose-dependent retrobulbar neuritis
• Requires baseline and monthly visual acuity/color discrimination testing.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Explain the role of Rifampin regarding the serum levels of methadone, warfarin, and oral contraceptives.
back:
• Potent CYP450 inducer (multiple isoforms)
• Increases hepatic metabolism of co-administered drugs
• Leads to subtherapeutic levels and clinical treatment failure.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
coreConcept: Metabolic Adverse Effects of RIPE Therapy
front: Contrast the metabolic laboratory abnormalities typically seen with Pyrazinamide (PZA) versus Isoniazid (INH).
back:
• PZA: Causes hyperuricemia (inhibits urate excretion) and hepatotoxicity
• INH: Causes elevated aminotransferases (hepatitis) without significant effect on uric acid.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Identify the harmless clinical sign associated with Rifampin that often causes patient anxiety regarding bodily secretions.
back:
• Orange discoloration of urine, sweat, tears, and saliva
• Can permanently stain soft contact lenses
• Benign side effect of the drug.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: The first-line antitubercular agent most likely to cause asymptomatic [___] due to inhibition of urate excretion is Pyrazinamide.
back:
• Hyperuricemia
• Occurs in nearly all patients taking PZA
• Only requires intervention if symptomatic gout develops.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: A 60-year-old male patient on triple-drug TB therapy develops jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. Which factor most significantly increases his risk for this complication during INH therapy?
back:
• Advanced age (risk is 2.3% in patients > 50)
• Alcohol consumption
• Preexisting liver disease.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Explain the biochemical basis for Isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy.
back:
• INH is structurally related to pyridoxine (B6)
• It promotes renal excretion of B6
• B6 deficiency interferes with normal nerve function.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Contrast Rifampin and Rifabutin regarding their use in HIV-co-infected patients receiving Protease Inhibitors (PIs).
back:
• Rifampin: Strong CYP inducer; lowers PI levels drastically (avoid)
• Rifabutin: Less potent CYP inducer; preferred for HIV/TB co-infection.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Identify the specific limitation that precludes the use of Ethambutol in young children (e.g., < 5 years old).
back:
• Inability to monitor visual changes accurately
• Children cannot reliably report color vision loss or blurred vision.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: To prevent peripheral neuropathy in patients receiving Isoniazid, clinicians should co-administer [___].
back:
• Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
• Required due to INH-promoted excretion of the vitamin
• Especially critical in slow acetylators, alcoholics, or patients with AIDS.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: A 52-year-old patient on RIPE therapy for pulmonary TB reports new difficulty distinguishing red from green traffic lights. Which drug is likely responsible?
back:
• Ethambutol
• Causes dose-related retrobulbar neuritis
• Manifests as decreased visual acuity and red-green color blindness.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Explain the pharmacodynamic mechanism by which Rifampin decreases the efficacy of concurrent medications like methadone and anticoagulants.
back:
• Potent induction of most cytochrome P450 isoforms (CYP1A2, 2C9, 2C19, 2D6, 3A4)
• Increases the metabolic elimination of co-administered drugs
• Leads to subtherapeutic serum concentrations.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
coreConcept: Metabolic Adverse Effects of TB Drugs
front: Contrast the metabolic side effect of Pyrazinamide with the metabolic concern associated with Isoniazid in patients with certain enzyme deficiencies.
back:
• Pyrazinamide: Causes uniform hyperuricemia (inhibits uric acid excretion)
• Isoniazid: Provokes hemolysis in patients with Glucose-6-Phosphate Dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Identify the specific dosing parameter associated with the development of a 'flu-like syndrome' (fever, chills, myalgias) during Rifampin therapy.
back:
• Administration less frequently than twice weekly (intermittent dosing)
• Often accompanied by anemia and thrombocytopenia.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: The harmless orange-to-red discoloration of sweat, tears, and urine is a signature side effect of [___].
back:
• Rifampin
• Can permanently stain soft contact lenses
• Clinical significance is minimal beyond patient reassurance.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: A 60-year-old chronic alcoholic starting TB treatment presents with jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. Which drug is the most likely cause and is age-dependent in its toxicity?
back:
• Isoniazid
• Causes clinical hepatitis (hepatocellular damage)
• Risk increases with age (>50 years) and alcohol consumption.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Describe the physiological reason for monitoring baseline and monthly visual acuity in patients receiving Ethambutol.
back:
• Early detection of retrobulbar neuritis
• High doses (25 mg/kg) increase risk
• Relies on subjective reporting; difficult in children.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Contrast the primary laboratory monitoring requirement for Pyrazinamide versus Ethambutol in a patient with renal insufficiency.
back:
• Pyrazinamide: Monitor liver enzymes (hepatotoxicity) and serum uric acid
• Ethambutol: Frequent visual testing (increased neuritis risk as drug is renally cleared).

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Which first-line antituberculosis drug is most associated with an asymptomatic rise in liver aminotransferases in up to 20% of patients?
back:
• Isoniazid
• Minor elevations (3-4x normal) usually asymptomatic
• Does not require drug cessation unless clinical hepatitis develops.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: To prevent peripheral neuropathy during isoniazid therapy, particularly in malnourished or diabetic patients, the clinician should co-administer [___].
back:
Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6).
• Isoniazid promotes the excretion of pyridoxine.
• Deficiency leads to nerve damage.
• Standard doses (10–50 mg/d) usually prevent this complication.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: A 50-year-old patient on a standard 4-drug TB regimen presents with difficulty reading small print and a new inability to distinguish red from green. Identify the causative agent.
back:
Ethambutol.
• Causes dose-dependent retrobulbar neuritis.
• Results in decreased visual acuity and color blindness.
• Requires baseline and monthly visual testing at higher dosages.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Explain the role of the Cytochrome P450 system in the metabolic drug interactions uniquely characteristic of Rifampin.
back:
Rifampin is a potent CYP450 inducer.
• It increases the metabolism of many drugs (e.g., warfarin, oral contraceptives, protease inhibitors).
• This leads to subtherapeutic serum levels of co-administered medications.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Contrast the management of asymptomatic transaminase elevation versus clinical hepatitis during Isoniazid treatment.
back:
Asymptomatic: Minor rise (up to 3–4x normal) occurs in 10–20%; usually does not require drug cessation.
• Clinical Hepatitis: Jaundice and RUQ pain occur in 1%; requires immediate, permanent drug discontinuation.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Identify the metabolic laboratory abnormality that uniformly occurs with Pyrazinamide use and its potential clinical complication.
back:
Hyperuricemia.
• PZA inhibits uric acid excretion.
• While often asymptomatic, it can trigger acute gouty arthritis.
• Asymptomatic cases generally do not require interruption of therapy.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: The development of a harmless orange discoloration of urine, sweat, and tears is a classic adverse feature of the 1st line drug [___].
back:
Rifampin.
• The drug and its metabolites are pigmented.
• Clinicians must warn patients to prevent alarm.
• It may permanently stain soft contact lenses.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: A 62-year-old chronic alcoholic being treated for TB develops deep jaundice and anorexia 4 weeks into therapy. Which 1st line drug is most statistically likely to cause this age-related toxicity?
back:
Isoniazid (INH).
• Risk of hepatitis increases significantly with age.
• Rare under age 20; exceeds 2.3% in patients over age 50.
• Alcoholism is a major independent potentiating risk factor.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Describe the specific dosing conditions under which Rifampin is likely to cause a 'Flu-like syndrome' and its associated symptoms.
back:
Occurs with intermittent dosing (less than twice weekly).
• Characterized by fever, chills, and myalgias.
• Can be associated with more serious reactions like thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, or acute tubular necrosis.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Contrast the ototoxicity patterns typically observed with Streptomycin regarding the vestibular and auditory systems.
back:
Streptomycin is primarily vestibulotoxic.
• Causes vertigo and loss of balance (often permanent).
• Auditory damage (hearing loss) is less common than with other aminoglycosides like neomycin or amikacin.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Which 1st line antituberculosis drug is most frequently associated with the development of drug-induced systemic lupus erythematosus?
back:
Isoniazid (INH).
• Can trigger the production of antinuclear antibodies.
• Presents with arthralgia, fever, and pleuritis.
• Symptoms typically resolve upon discontinuation of the drug.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: To prevent peripheral neuropathy in patients receiving isoniazid (INH) for tuberculosis, the patient should be co-administered [___].
back:
• Vitamin B6 (Pyridoxine)
• INH inhibits conversion of pyridoxine to its active form and promotes renal excretion
• Supplementation with 10–50 mg daily is mandatory to prevent neurological damage

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: A 40-year-old male on anti-TB therapy reports difficulty distinguishing between the red and green lights at traffic signals. Which drug is most likely responsible?
back:
• Ethambutol
• Causes dose-dependent retrobulbar optic neuritis
• Manifests as decreased visual acuity and red-green color blindness
• Requires monthly visual monitoring and is avoided in young children

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Explain how Rifampin causes therapeutic failure of oral contraceptive pills and warfarin.
back:
• Potent induction of hepatic cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzymes
• Increases oxidative metabolism of co-administered drugs
• Results in sub-therapeutic plasma levels and clinical treatment failure

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Contrast the hepatotoxic potential of Pyrazinamide with that of Ethambutol within the standard 1st line RIPE regimen.
back:
• Pyrazinamide: Considered the most hepatotoxic agent, frequently causing hepatic necrosis
• Ethambutol: Non-hepatotoxic agent
• Ethambutol is often the only drug continued during drug-induced liver injury

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Why must Pyrazinamide be used cautiously in patients with a history of acute gouty arthritis?
back:
• Inhibits renal secretion of uric acid
• Uniformly results in hyperuricemia in most patients
• May trigger acute gouty attacks or painful non-gouty polyarthralgias

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: A patient on anti-TB therapy presents with orange-colored urine, sweat, and tears. This is a harmless side effect of [___].
back:
• Rifampin
• Due to the physical properties of the drug and its metabolites
• Affects all secretions including saliva and contact lenses
• Reassurance is vital for compliance

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: A 65-year-old alcoholic male begins the RIPE regimen. Three weeks later, he develops jaundice and RUQ pain. Which drug's risk increases most significantly with his age and alcohol history?
back:
• Isoniazid (INH)
• Hepatotoxicity risk increases significantly with age (>35 years)
• Alcohol consumption induces enzymes that produce toxic INH metabolites, potentiating liver injury

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Describe the biochemical mechanism behind Isoniazid-induced sideroblastic anemia.
back:
• INH competes with pyridoxal phosphate for delta-aminolevulinic acid (d-ALA) synthase
• This blocks the rate-limiting step of heme synthesis
• Iron accumulates in mitochondria, producing characteristic ringed sideroblasts

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Contrast the primary dose-limiting toxicities of Streptomycin and Ethambutol.
back:
• Streptomycin: Ototoxicity (vestibular/auditory) and Nephrotoxicity
• Ethambutol: Optic toxicity (acuity/color vision)
• Streptomycin is given parenterally whereas Ethambutol is an oral medication

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Which first-line anti-tuberculosis agent is associated with a drug-induced Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) syndrome?
back:
• Isoniazid (INH)
• Presents with fever and arthralgias similar to idiopathic SLE
• Associated with anti-histone antibodies
• Risk is higher in slow acetylators

category: Describe the characteristic pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetic properties of Rifampin, Isoniazid, Ethambutol and Pyrazinamide
front: Isoniazid exerts its bactericidal effect by inhibiting the synthesis of [___], which are essential lipid components of the mycobacterial cell wall.
back:
* Mycolic acids.
* These essential lipids are unique to the mycobacterial cell wall; their inhibition leads to bacterial death in actively growing organisms.

category: Describe the characteristic pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetic properties of Rifampin, Isoniazid, Ethambutol and Pyrazinamide
front: A patient on a standard anti-tuberculosis regimen develops peripheral neuropathy and ataxia. This toxicity is most likely occurring because the patient has a genetic polymorphism affecting which metabolic process?
back:
* Slow acetylation.
* Genetically determined low activity of N-acetyltransferase reduces Isoniazid clearance, increasing drug levels and the risk of pyridoxine deficiency-related neurotoxicity.

category: Describe the characteristic pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetic properties of Rifampin, Isoniazid, Ethambutol and Pyrazinamide
front: Explain the role of the mycobacterial KatG enzyme in the pharmacodynamics of Isoniazid.
back:
* KatG is a catalase-peroxidase enzyme.
* It acts as a bioactivator that converts Isoniazid (a prodrug) into its active form to inhibit cell wall synthesis.

category: Describe the characteristic pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetic properties of Rifampin, Isoniazid, Ethambutol and Pyrazinamide
front: Contrast the specific enzymatic targets of Ethambutol and Isoniazid during mycobacterial cell wall assembly.
back:
* Ethambutol: Inhibits arabinosyl transferases (embCAB operon), blocking the polymerization of arabinoglycan.
* Isoniazid: Inhibits acyl carrier protein reductase (InhA) and beta-ketoacyl carrier protein synthetase (KasA).

category: Describe the characteristic pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetic properties of Rifampin, Isoniazid, Ethambutol and Pyrazinamide
front: Identify the primary pharmacokinetic effect of Rifampin on the cytochrome P450 system and its clinical significance.
back:
* Potent induction of CYP450 isoforms (e.g., 3A4, 2C9, 2D6).
* Clinical significance: Markedly decreases the serum levels and efficacy of drugs like warfarin, oral contraceptives, and protease inhibitors.

category: Describe the characteristic pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetic properties of Rifampin, Isoniazid, Ethambutol and Pyrazinamide
front: Pyrazinamide is a prodrug converted into its active form, [___], by the mycobacterial enzyme [___].
back:
* Active metabolite: Pyrazinoic acid.
* Converting enzyme: Pyrazinamidase (encoded by pncA).
* Resistance arises from pncA mutations that prevent this metabolic activation.

category: Describe the characteristic pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetic properties of Rifampin, Isoniazid, Ethambutol and Pyrazinamide
front: A TB patient with a creatinine clearance of 25 mL/min is starting therapy. Which first-line agent requires a dose reduction or interval adjustment specifically to prevent dose-related retrobulbar neuritis?
back:
* Ethambutol.
* Because it is primarily renally excreted (50% unchanged), it accumulates in renal failure, increasing the risk of optic nerve toxicity.

category: Describe the characteristic pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetic properties of Rifampin, Isoniazid, Ethambutol and Pyrazinamide
front: Describe how the acidic environment of macrophage lysosomes (pH 5.5) influences the pharmacodynamics of Pyrazinamide.
back:
* Pyrazinamide is inactive at neutral pH.
* Lysosomal acidity facilitates drug activation, allowing it to effectively disrupt membrane metabolism in intracellular mycobacteria.

category: Describe the characteristic pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetic properties of Rifampin, Isoniazid, Ethambutol and Pyrazinamide
front: Contrast the primary routes of elimination for Rifampin and Ethambutol.
back:
* Rifampin: Primarily hepatic/biliary excretion; undergoes enterohepatic recirculation and turns secretions orange.
* Ethambutol: Primarily renal elimination; approx. 50% is excreted unchanged in the urine.

category: Describe the characteristic pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetic properties of Rifampin, Isoniazid, Ethambutol and Pyrazinamide
front: Identify the impact of a high-fat meal on the peak plasma concentration (Cmax) of Isoniazid.
back:
* Cmax is decreased by up to 50%.
* Absorption is optimal on an empty stomach; patients should avoid fatty meals to ensure therapeutic levels.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Isoniazid induces peripheral neuropathy by promoting the excretion of [___], leading to a relative deficiency.
back:
• Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
• Required as a co-factor in nerve function
• Toxicity is reversed by B6 supplementation
• More common in slow acetylators or alcoholics.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: A 50-year-old patient on antituberculosis therapy reports blurred vision and difficulty distinguishing red from green. Which drug and specific toxicity are likely responsible?
back:
• Ethambutol
• Retrobulbar neuritis
• Dose-dependent (usually >25 mg/kg/d)
• Requires baseline and monthly visual acuity and color discrimination testing.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Explain the pharmacological mechanism by which Rifampin reduces the efficacy of concurrent medications like methadone or oral contraceptives.
back:
• Potent induction of Cytochrome P450 (CYP3A4, 2C9, etc.)
• Increases metabolism/elimination of co-administered drugs
• Results in subtherapeutic serum concentrations of substrates.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Contrast the typical hepatotoxic presentation of Isoniazid with that of Rifampin.
back:
• Isoniazid: Hepatocellular damage/necrosis; risk increases with age and alcohol use.
• Rifampin: Cholestatic jaundice and hepatitis; imparts harmless orange discoloration to body fluids.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Identify the primary clinical monitoring requirement for a patient with a history of gout starting Pyrazinamide.
back:
• Serum uric acid levels
• Drug inhibits urate excretion
• Causes uniform hyperuricemia
• Usually asymptomatic but can provoke acute gouty arthritis.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: The 'flu-like syndrome' characterized by fever, chills, and myalgias is specifically associated with [___] when administered less frequently than twice weekly.
back:
• Rifampin
• Occurs during intermittent dosing regimens
• May be accompanied by thrombocytopenia and anemia
• Resolves with more frequent dosing.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: A patient with TB develops joint pains, fever, and a malar rash after 8 weeks of therapy. Which first-line agent is the most likely cause of this immunologic reaction?
back:
• Isoniazid (INH)
• Drug-induced Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)
• Characterized by antinuclear antibodies
• Resolves upon drug discontinuation.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Describe the physiological process leading to Isoniazid-induced hepatitis and identify the patient group at highest risk.
back:
• First-pass hepatic acetylation produces toxic metabolites
• Risk increases significantly over age 50 (2.3% incidence)
• Potentiated by alcohol dependence and the postpartum period.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Contrast the renal adverse effects of Ethambutol with those of Rifampin.
back:
• Ethambutol: Minimal renal risk, but dose must be reduced in failure to prevent accumulation.
• Rifampin: Risk of acute tubular necrosis and interstitial nephritis.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Identify the 'sterilizing agent' among first-line TB drugs that is active against intracellular organisms in acidic lysosomes but limited by 1-5% hepatotoxicity.
back:
• Pyrazinamide (PZA)
• Active at pH 5.5
• Key for shortening therapy duration to 6 months
• Common side effects include nausea and vomiting.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy is primarily prevented by the co-administration of [___].
back:
● Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
● Prevents relative deficiency as INH promotes its renal excretion
● Essential for patients with predisposing conditions (alcoholism, diabetes, pregnancy).

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: A 45-year-old TB patient reports his urine and tears have turned orange since starting treatment. Which 1st line drug is responsible and what is the clinical significance?
back:
● Rifampin
● Clinical Significance: Harmless side effect
● Soft contact lenses may be permanently stained
● Potent inducer of Cytochrome P450 enzymes.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Explain the mechanism by which Pyrazinamide (PZA) causes joint pain in patients during the intensive phase of TB therapy.
back:
● Hyperuricemia
● Mechanism: PZA inhibits the renal secretion of uric acid
● Can precipitate acute gouty arthritis in susceptible individuals.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Contrast the primary ocular toxicity of Ethambutol with the harmless ocular effect of Rifampin.
back:
● Ethambutol: Retrobulbar neuritis (decreased acuity, red-green color blindness)
● Rifampin: Harmless orange staining of tears
● Ethambutol requires monthly visual monitoring; Rifampin does not.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Which 1st line antituberculosis drug is most likely to cause a 'flu-like syndrome' if administered intermittently (less than twice weekly)?
back:
● Rifampin
● Features: Fever, chills, myalgias, and anemia
● Occurs specifically with intermittent or irregular dosing schedules.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: The risk of Isoniazid-induced [___] is highest in rapid acetylators when taking the drug once-weekly, but clinical hepatitis risk is generally higher with [___].
back:
● Subtherapeutic concentrations; Advancing age
● Hepatitis risk: rare under age 20, rises to 2.3% in those over age 50
● Alcoholism also significantly increases hepatitis risk.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: A patient on RIPE therapy presents with jaundice, nausea, and right upper quadrant pain. Which three drugs in the regimen are the most likely causes of this presentation?
back:
● Isoniazid, Rifampin, and Pyrazinamide
● Collectively known as the hepatotoxic trio
● Ethambutol is notably spared from causing hepatocellular damage.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Directly explain the management of a patient who develops minor increases in liver aminotransferases (3x normal) while on Isoniazid without symptoms.
back:
● Continue therapy with close monitoring
● Minor elevations occur in 10-20% and are often transient
● Stop immediately only if clinical hepatitis or jaundice develops.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Contrast the dose-related toxicity of Ethambutol at 15 mg/kg versus 25 mg/kg dosages.
back:
● 15 mg/kg: Visual disturbances in ~2% of patients
● 25 mg/kg: Significantly higher risk of retrobulbar neuritis
● Higher doses are contraindicated in children too young for vision testing.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Identify the 1st line drug that is an analog of nicotinamide and is associated with photosensitivity.
back:
● Pyrazinamide (PZA)
● Adverse effects: Hepatotoxicity, hyperuricemia, drug fever, and photosensitivity
● Acts as a 'sterilizing agent' against intracellular organisms.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: The primary mechanism behind Isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy is a clinical deficiency of [___].
back:
- Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6).
- Isoniazid promotes the excretion of this vitamin, leading to nerve damage.
- Supplementation (25-50 mg/day) prevents this toxicity.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: A 52-year-old male with a history of alcohol dependence undergoes therapy for pulmonary tuberculosis. Two months later, he presents with jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. The first-line drug most likely responsible for this hepatitis in an older patient is [___].
back:
- Isoniazid (INH).
- Risk of INH-induced hepatitis increases with age (>2.3% in those over 50) and alcohol consumption.
- It is the most common major toxic effect of INH.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Explain the specific impact of Ethambutol on ocular health during tuberculosis treatment.
back:
- Causes dose-related retrobulbar neuritis.
- Manifests as decreased visual acuity and loss of red-green color discrimination.
- Requires baseline and monthly vision monitoring.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Contrast the hepatic adverse effects commonly associated with Rifampin versus Pyrazinamide.
back:
- Rifampin: Primarily causes cholestatic jaundice and occasionally hepatitis.
- Pyrazinamide: Causes hepatocellular damage/hepatitis (occurring in 1-5% of patients).

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Identify the harmless, non-toxic adverse effect of Rifampin that requires early patient counseling to prevent non-compliance.
back:
- Orange-red discoloration of body fluids.
- Affects urine, sweat, and tears.
- Can permanently stain soft contact lenses.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: The first-line antituberculosis agent that uniformly causes asymptomatic [___] in nearly all patients is Pyrazinamide.
back:
- Hyperuricemia.
- Pyrazinamide interferes with uric acid excretion; may occasionally provoke acute gouty arthritis.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: A 40-year-old patient on a twice-weekly antituberculosis regimen develops sudden fever, chills, and myalgias shortly after ingestion. This clinical 'flu-like syndrome' is specific to the intermittent use of [___].
back:
- Rifampin.
- Occurs when the drug is administered less than twice weekly.
- May be associated with thrombocytopenia and anemia.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Describe the immunologic reaction occasionally seen with Isoniazid that resembles a multisystem connective tissue disorder.
back:
- Drug-induced Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE).
- Manifests as fever, joint pains, and skin rashes.
- Associated with the formation of antinuclear antibodies (ANA).

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Contrast the diagnostic reasons for avoiding Ethambutol in young children compared to Isoniazid.
back:
- Ethambutol: Avoided because young children cannot reliably report visual acuity or color vision changes (retrobulbar neuritis).
- Isoniazid: Generally safe in children; hepatitis risk is extremely low under age 20.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Which first-line antituberculosis drug is most frequently associated with light-chain proteinuria and acute tubular necrosis?
back:
- Rifampin.
- Renal effects can also include interstitial nephritis.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: To prevent peripheral neuropathy in a patient receiving Isoniazid (INH), clinicians should routinely co-administer [___].
back:
- Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
- Isoniazid promotes pyridoxine excretion, leading to deficiency
- Deficiency manifests as sensory disturbances and paresthesias
- Recommended prophylaxis: 25–50 mg daily

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: A 55-year-old male on anti-tuberculosis therapy presents with anorexia, nausea, and right upper quadrant pain. Laboratory tests show significantly elevated aminotransferases. Which three 1st line drugs are primarily responsible for this hepatotoxicity?
back:
- Isoniazid (INH), Rifampin (RIF), and Pyrazinamide (PZA)
- These agents cause chemical or idiosyncratic drug-induced hepatitis
- Hepatotoxicity risk increases with age and alcohol consumption
- Offending drugs must be discontinued immediately

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Explain the biological mechanism underlying the harmless orange discoloration of body fluids in patients taking Rifampin.
back:
- Rifampin is a macrocyclic antibiotic possessing an intrinsic reddish-orange pigment
- The drug and its metabolites are physically excreted via urine, sweat, and tears
- It is a benign pharmacokinetic property, not an indication of toxicity

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
coreConcept: Toxicity Profiles of Ethambutol vs. Isoniazid
front: Contrast the visual toxicities associated with Ethambutol versus the potential neurologic toxicities of Isoniazid.
back:
- Ethambutol: Causes retrobulbar neuritis (red-green color blindness, decreased visual acuity)
- Isoniazid: Causes peripheral neuropathy (paresthesias) and CNS effects (memory loss, psychosis)
- Ethambutol toxicity is dose-dependent; Isoniazid toxicity is due to pyridoxine deficiency

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Describe the clinical features and predisposing factors of the "flu-like syndrome" associated with Rifampin.
back:
- Features: Fever, chills, myalgias, anemia, and thrombocytopenia
- Predisposing factor: Occurs when Rifampin is administered intermittently (less than twice weekly)
- Management: Requires changing to a daily or more frequent dosing schedule

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: The 1st line antituberculosis drug most frequently associated with the development of asymptomatic hyperuricemia and arthralgia is [___].
back:
- Pyrazinamide (PZA)
- It inhibits the renal excretion of urates
- Leads to uric acid accumulation, which can trigger arthralgia
- Clinical gout is rare but requires permanent discontinuation if it occurs

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: A patient on a standard four-drug regimen for tuberculosis complains of difficulty distinguishing traffic light colors. Identify the offending agent and the mandatory clinical monitoring required.
back:
- Offending Agent: Ethambutol (EMB)
- Mechanism: Dose-related retrobulbar neuritis
- Monitoring: Baseline and monthly visual acuity and red-green color discrimination testing
- Contraindication: Relative in children too young for reliable testing

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Describe the drug interaction mechanism by which Rifampin reduces the efficacy of oral contraceptives and warfarin.
back:
- Potent induction of multiple hepatic cytochrome P450 isoforms (CYP3A4, 2C9)
- Significantly increases the metabolic clearance rate of these substrates
- Results in subtherapeutic plasma concentrations and potential clinical failure

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Distinguish between the hepatic effects of Isoniazid regarding asymptomatic enzyme elevation versus clinical hepatitis management.
back:
- Asymptomatic Elevation: Minor aminotransferase increase (up to 20% of patients); continuation is acceptable
- Clinical Hepatitis: Symptoms like jaundice or RUQ pain; requires immediate permanent discontinuation
- Risk increases significantly in patients over age 35

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Name the 1st line antituberculosis drug that is relatively contraindicated in young children due to the difficulty of performing reliable ophthalmologic assessments.
back:
- Ethambutol (EMB)
- Children cannot accurately report changes in visual acuity or color vision
- Failure to monitor risks permanent, irreversible retrobulbar neuritis
- Isoniazid or Rifampin are preferred when possible in pediatrics

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy is primarily caused by the drug-promoted deficiency and renal excretion of [___].
back: * Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6). * INH forms hydrazones with B6, leading to functional deficiency. * Supplementary B6 (10-50 mg/day) prevents this toxicity.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: A 48-year-old male on anti-tubercular therapy presents with a decrease in visual acuity and difficulty distinguishing between red and green. Which medication is likely responsible?
back: * Ethambutol. * Causes dose-related retrobulbar neuritis. * Requires baseline and monthly visual acuity and color discrimination testing.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Explain the metabolic mechanism by which Rifampin reduces the plasma levels of co-administered drugs like warfarin and oral contraceptives.
back: * Potent induction of Cytochrome P450 (CYP) isoforms (3A4, 2C9, 2C19, 2D6). * Increases the metabolic clearance of several drugs. * Enhances enterohepatic recirculation elimination.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Contrast the primary patterns of hepatotoxicity associated with Isoniazid versus Rifampin.
back: * Isoniazid: Age-related hepatocellular necrosis (clinical hepatitis). * Rifampin: Predominantly cholestatic jaundice and induction of light-chain proteinuria.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: How should a clinician manage a patient who develops asymptomatic hyperuricemia during a standard course of Pyrazinamide?
back: * Continue therapy without adjustment. * Hyperuricemia occurs uniformly due to inhibited renal urate secretion. * Cessation is only required if symptomatic gout develops.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: The characteristic harmless orange-red discoloration of urine, sweat, and tears is a classic adverse effect of [___].
back: * Rifampin. * Due to the physical properties of the drug and its metabolites. * Patients should be warned to avoid permanent staining of soft contact lenses.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: A patient on a 4-drug TB regimen develops a maculopapular rash, joint pain, and a malar eruption. Laboratory tests confirm drug-induced Systemic Lupus Erythematosus. Which agent is the most likely cause?
back: * Isoniazid (INH). * Classically associated with drug-induced lupus. * Symptoms usually resolve upon drug discontinuation.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Describe the biochemical mechanism by which Pyrazinamide increases serum uric acid levels.
back: * Its active metabolite, pyrazinoic acid, inhibits the renal tubular secretion of uric acid. * This leads to urate retention. * This occurs specifically in the acidic environment of lysosomes.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Contrast 'minor transaminitis' with 'clinical hepatitis' in the context of Isoniazid therapy.
back: * Minor transaminitis: 10-20% incidence; asymptomatic; continue therapy. * Clinical hepatitis: 1% incidence; symptomatic (jaundice, RUQ pain); requires immediate and permanent drug cessation.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Identify the first-line antituberculosis agent most frequently associated with phototoxicity and dose-limiting gastric irritation.
back: * Pyrazinamide (PZA). * Can also cause nongouty polyarthralgia. * Known as a 'sterilizing' agent against intracellular bacilli.

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: The most common and significant major toxic effect of Isoniazid (INH) is [___].
back:
● Hepatitis / Hepatocellular damage
● Risk increases with age and alcohol consumption
● Development contraindicates further drug use

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: A 45-year-old patient on antituberculosis therapy presents with 'burning feet' and paresthesias in a 'glove and stocking' distribution. This pathophysiology is caused by a relative deficiency of [___].
back:
● Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
● INH promotes renal excretion of B6
● Results in peripheral sensory neuropathy

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Explain the clinical significance of hyperuricemia observed during treatment with Pyrazinamide.
back:
● Occurs uniformly in most patients
● Usually asymptomatic and harmless
● Not a reason to discontinue therapy unless acute gouty arthritis occurs

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Contrast the primary sensory toxicities of Ethambutol with those of Streptomycin.
back:
● Ethambutol: Visual toxicity (retrobulbar neuritis, red-green color blindness)
● Streptomycin: Auditory/Vestibular toxicity (ototoxicity, vertigo, hearing loss)

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Identify the characteristic harmless side effect of Rifampin that often causes patient anxiety regarding bodily fluids.
back:
● Orange discoloration of urine, sweat, and tears
● Can permanently stain soft contact lenses
● Clinically benign and expected

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: To prevent the development of peripheral neuropathy, Isoniazid must be administered alongside [___].
back:
● Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
● Recommended dose: 10–50 mg/day
● Especially critical in diabetics, alcoholics, and malnourished patients

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: A patient undergoing TB treatment reports difficulty reading and inability to distinguish traffic light colors. This presentation is most characteristic of toxicity from [___].
back:
● Ethambutol
● Causes dose-dependent retrobulbar neuritis
● Monthly visual acuity and color testing is recommended

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Describe the biochemical mechanism by which Isoniazid interferes with nerve function.
back:
● INH promotes the renal excretion of pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
● Resulting deficiency interferes with the integrity of peripheral nerves
● Reversible by supplemental B6 administration

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Distinguish between the typical hepatic adverse effect patterns of Isoniazid and Rifampin.
back:
● Isoniazid: Hepatocellular damage and necrosis (mimics viral hepatitis)
● Rifampin: Primarily associated with cholestatic jaundice and elevated bilirubin

category: Discuss the adverse effects of 1st line antituberculosis drugs
front: Identify the primary clinical limitation preventing the safe use of Ethambutol in young children.
back:
● Inability to accurately monitor visual acuity and color discrimination
● High risk of undetected, irreversible retrobulbar neuritis

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: The standard WHO-recommended treatment for newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis consists of a 2-month intensive phase followed by a [___]-month continuation phase.
back:
• 4 months.
• Intensive Phase: Isoniazid, Rifampin, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol.
• Continuation Phase: Isoniazid and Rifampin.
• Total duration: 6 months.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: A 35-year-old HIV-positive male starting a protease-inhibitor-based antiretroviral regimen is diagnosed with pulmonary TB. To minimize CYP450 induction while treating TB, Rifampin should be replaced with [___].
back:
• Rifabutin.
• Less potent inducer of cytochrome P450 enzymes.
• Minimizes reductions in antiretroviral drug levels compared to Rifampin.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Explain the clinical role and specific enzymatic target of Bedaquiline in the management of tuberculosis.
back:
• Inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase.
• Indicated for adults with Multidrug-Resistant TB (MDR-TB).
• Used for 24 weeks in combination with at least three other active drugs.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Contrast the continuation phase duration for standard drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis with cases presenting with initial cavitation and positive cultures at month two.
back:
• Standard: 4 months (6 months total).
• Cavitary/Culture-positive: 7 months (9 months total).
• Extension prevents relapse in patients with high bacillary burden.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Which specific drug combination and dosing frequency are recommended for the 3-month short-course treatment of latent tuberculosis infection (LTBI)?
back:
• Rifapentine and Isoniazid.
• Dosed at 900 mg each.
• Frequency: Once weekly for 12 weeks.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: When using Isoniazid as monotherapy for the standard treatment of latent tuberculosis infection, the total duration of therapy is [___] months.
back:
• 9 months.
• 300 mg daily (or 900 mg twice weekly).
• Effectively prevents progression to active disease.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: A patient with Multidrug-Resistant TB is initiated on Bedaquiline. Identify the essential baseline cardiac screening required for this agent and the clinical rationale.
back:
• Electrocardiogram (ECG).
• Rationale: Monitor for QTc prolongation.
• Bedaquiline carries a black-box warning for cardiac conduction risks.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Explain the pharmacodynamic role of Pyrazinamide during the 2-month intensive phase of tuberculosis treatment.
back:
• Acts as a "sterilizing" agent.
• Targets intracellular bacilli in acidic macrophage lysosomes.
• Allows reduction of total treatment duration from 9 to 6 months.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Contrast the Rifampin monotherapy protocol for latent TB with the standard Isoniazid monotherapy protocol.
back:
• Rifampin: 600 mg daily for 4 months.
• Isoniazid: 300 mg daily for 9 months.
• Rifampin is an alternative for Isoniazid intolerance or exposure to INH-resistant strains.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: List the four agents utilized in the first-line "RIPE" intensive phase for newly diagnosed pulmonary TB.
back:
• Rifampin (RIF).
• Isoniazid (INH).
• Pyrazinamide (PZA).
• Ethambutol (EMB).

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: The standard WHO intensive phase treatment for a patient with newly diagnosed, drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis consists of [___] administered for two months.
back:
● Isoniazid (INH)
● Rifampin (RIF)
● Pyrazinamide (PZA)
● Ethambutol (EMB)

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
coreConcept: Rifamycin Drug Interactions in HIV/TB Co-infection
front: A 35-year-old HIV-positive male on a Protease Inhibitor-based antiretroviral regimen is diagnosed with pulmonary TB. Why is Rifabutin preferred over Rifampin in this scenario?
back:
● Rifampin is a potent CYP450 inducer that significantly lowers Protease Inhibitor levels.
● Rifabutin is a less potent inducer, allowing for safer co-administration with reduced risk of subtherapeutic ARV levels.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Explain the physiological conversion of Pyrazinamide required for its anti-mycobacterial activity within the host.
back:
● Converted to pyrazinoic acid by mycobacterial pyrazinamidase (encoded by pncA).
● Active specifically in acidic environments, such as macrophage lysosomes.
● Disrupts mycobacterial cell membrane metabolism and transport.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Contrast the standard continuation phase duration for pulmonary TB in a patient with a non-cavitary initial X-ray versus one with cavitary disease and positive 2-month cultures.
back:
● Non-cavitary: 4 months of Isoniazid and Rifampin (total 6 months).
● Cavitary + 2-month culture positive: 7 months of Isoniazid and Rifampin (total 9 months) to prevent relapse.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Identify the specific second-line oxazolidinone agent used for Multidrug-Resistant TB (MDR-TB) that is limited by dose-dependent marrow suppression and peripheral neuropathy.
back:
● Linezolid.
● Side effects include thrombocytopenia, anemia, and irreversible optic/peripheral neuropathy with prolonged use.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: In the management of Latent TB (LTBI), a common short-course preventive regimen consists of 12 once-weekly doses of Isoniazid and [___].
back:
● Rifapentine.
● Used for 3 months total.
● Offers improved compliance compared to 9-month Isoniazid monotherapy.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: A patient undergoing therapy for pulmonary TB develops jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. What is the immediate clinical protocol regarding their medication?
back:
● Discontinue hepatotoxic drugs immediately (Isoniazid, Rifampin, Pyrazinamide).
● Monitor serum aminotransferases until symptoms resolve and levels return to baseline or <2x normal.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: How does the pharmacological addition of Bedaquiline specifically target Multidrug-Resistant (MDR-TB) strains?
back:
● Inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase, a novel target distinct from first-line drugs.
● Active against both replicating and nonreplicating bacilli.
● Indicated when the isolate is resistant to both Isoniazid and Rifampin.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Contrast the treatment of Latent TB (LTBI) with the treatment of Newly Diagnosed Pulmonary TB regarding drug quantity and objectives.
back:
● LTBI: Single-drug therapy (e.g., Rifampin 4 months or INH 9 months); goal is to prevent progression to active disease.
● Pulmonary TB: Multi-drug therapy (4 drugs); goal is to cure infection and prevent emergence of resistance.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: What is the primary role of Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) supplementation during standard Isoniazid therapy?
back:
● Prevents peripheral neuropathy.
● Isoniazid promotes the excretion of pyridoxine, especially in slow acetylators or patients with diabetes/alcoholism.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: The standard intensive phase for newly diagnosed drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis consists of a four-drug combination of Isoniazid, Rifampin, Pyrazinamide, and [___] for a duration of 2 months.
back:
• Ethambutol
• Purpose: Prevents emergence of resistance to Isoniazid or Rifampin
• Ovicidal effects are not seen in mycobacteria; it inhibits arabinosyl transferase.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: A 30-year-old patient with pulmonary TB has completed 2 months of HRZE. Follow-up sputum smear is negative. Identify the drugs and duration recommended for the next phase of WHO standard management.
back:
• Drugs: Isoniazid and Rifampin (Continuation phase)
• Duration: 4 months
• Total treatment duration: 6 months for most patients.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Explain the role of Pyrazinamide in allowing the shortening of tuberculosis treatment from 9 months to 6 months.
back:
• Acts as a 'sterilizing agent'
• Targets semi-dormant bacilli in acidic environments (macrophage lysosomes)
• Highly effective during the initial 2-month inflammatory phase.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Contrast the management approach for a patient diagnosed with Latent Tuberculosis Infection (LTBI) versus one with Multidrug-Resistant TB (MDR-TB).
back:
• LTBI: Monotherapy; typically Isoniazid (9 months) or Rifampin (4 months)
• MDR-TB: Resistant to INH + RIF; requires ≥4 second-line drugs (e.g., Bedaquiline, Linezolid) for 18–24 months.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Specify the clinical criteria under which the continuation phase of drug-susceptible TB treatment should be extended from 4 to 7 months.
back:
• Cavitation visible on the initial chest radiograph
• Positive sputum cultures at the end of the 2-month intensive phase.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: In the management of Multidrug-Resistant TB (MDR-TB), the strict WHO definition requires the isolate to be resistant to at least [___] and [___].
back:
• Isoniazid
• Rifampin

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: An HIV-infected patient is diagnosed with pulmonary TB and is currently taking a protease inhibitor-based ARV regimen. What substitution is mandatory to avoid major drug-drug interactions?
back:
• Replace Rifampin with Rifabutin
• Rationale: Rifabutin is a less potent inducer of Cytochrome P450, minimizing clearance of protease inhibitors.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Explain the biological mechanism by which Bedaquiline acts against resistant strains of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
back:
• Inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase
• Targets both replicating and non-replicating bacilli
• Reserved for MDR-TB due to risks of QTc prolongation and mortality.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Contrast the standard daily Isoniazid regimen for Latent TB with the Rifapentine-based alternative regimen regarding duration and frequency.
back:
• Isoniazid: Daily dosing for 9 months
• Isoniazid + Rifapentine: Once-weekly dosing for 3 months (12 doses total)
• Rifapentine regimen improves compliance due to shorter duration.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Identify the specific second-line TB drug that requires mandatory Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) co-administration to prevent central nervous system toxicity.
back:
• Cycloserine (and Isoniazid/Ethionamide)
• Ameliorates neurologic toxicities like depression, psychosis, and seizures.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: The standard WHO-recommended 6-month regimen for newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis consists of a 2-month initial phase using Rifampin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, and [___].
back:
• Ethambutol
• This four-drug intensive phase targets rapidly multiplying and dormant bacilli to prevent resistance development.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: A 28-year-old patient on anti-tuberculosis therapy presents with decreased visual acuity and loss of red-green color discrimination. Which drug should be immediately discontinued?
back:
• Ethambutol
• Causes dose-related retrobulbar neuritis
• Requires baseline and monthly visual acuity/color testing.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Explain the role of the mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase enzyme (KatG) in the efficacy of Isoniazid therapy.
back:
• KatG activates the Isoniazid prodrug into its active metabolite
• The active form inhibits mycolic acid synthesis
• Deletion/mutation of KatG is a primary mechanism of high-level resistance.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Contrast the treatment duration and drug selection for Latent Tuberculosis Infection (LTBI) versus standard Active Pulmonary Tuberculosis.
back:
• Latent TB: Monotherapy with Isoniazid (9 months) or Rifampin (4 months)
• Active TB: Combination therapy (RIPE) for 6 months minimum
• Latent therapy prevents reactivation; Active therapy treats symptomatic disease.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Define the specific diagnostic criteria for Multidrug-Resistant Tuberculosis (MDR-TB).
back:
• Resistance to at least Isoniazid and Rifampin simultaneously
• Requires treatment with second-line agents (e.g., Fluoroquinolones, Bedaquiline, Linezolid).

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Pyrazinamide is uniquely effective against mycobacteria residing within the [___] environment of macrophage lysosomes.
back:
• Acidic (low pH)
• It acts as a 'sterilizing' agent against residual intracellular organisms
• Most active during the first 2 months of therapy.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: A patient with HIV is being treated for TB. Rifabutin is often substituted for Rifampin because Rifabutin [___].
back:
• Is a less potent inducer of Cytochrome P450 enzymes
• Prevents subtherapeutic levels of Protease Inhibitors or NNRTIs
• Minimizes complex drug-drug interactions.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Describe the molecular mechanism by which Rifampin inhibits the replication of Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
back:
• Binds to the beta subunit of bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase
• Blocks RNA synthesis and transcription
• Resistance occurs via rpoB gene point mutations.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Contrast the adverse effect profiles of Isoniazid and Pyrazinamide regarding metabolic byproducts.
back:
• Isoniazid: Causes peripheral neuropathy via relative Pyridoxine (B6) deficiency
• Pyrazinamide: Causes hyperuricemia (asymptomatic in most) and potentially gouty arthritis.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Identify the novel second-line agent for MDR-TB that acts by inhibiting mycobacterial ATP synthase.
back:
• Bedaquiline
• Used only when other regimens fail
• Side effects include QTc prolongation and hepatotoxicity.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: For newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, the standard WHO-recommended intensive phase consists of a four-drug regimen containing [___] for a duration of 2 months.
back:
• Isoniazid (INH)
• Rifampin (RIF)
• Pyrazinamide (PZA)
• Ethambutol (EMB)

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: A 30-year-old patient with no comorbidities is diagnosed with drug-susceptible pulmonary TB. Following a successful 2-month intensive phase, the standard continuation phase duration and drugs used are [___].
back:
• Duration: 4 months
• Drugs: Isoniazid and Rifampin
• Total treatment duration: 6 months

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Explain the pharmacodynamic role of adding Pyrazinamide (PZA) to the initial 2 months of tuberculosis therapy.
back:
• Acts as a 'sterilizing' agent
• Kills residual intracellular organisms in acidic lysosomes
• Allows shortening total therapy from 9 months to 6 months

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Contrast the WHO-recommended intensive phase for standard pulmonary TB with the criteria defining Multidrug-Resistant Tuberculosis (MDR-TB).
back:
• Standard: Susceptibility to all first-line agents (HRZE)
• MDR-TB: Resistance to at least Isoniazid and Rifampin
• MDR-TB requires second-line agents (e.g., Bedaquiline, Fluoroquinolones)

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Identify the novel diarylquinoline agent specifically indicated for the 24-week treatment of adults with pulmonary MDR-TB by inhibiting mycobacterial ATP synthase.
back:
• Bedaquiline
• Used with at least 3 other active drugs
• Requires monitoring for QTc prolongation

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: The standard protocol for latent tuberculosis (LTB) in a patient who cannot tolerate Isoniazid involves the daily administration of [___] for a duration of 4 months.
back:
• Rifampin (600 mg daily)
• Alternative: Isoniazid + Rifapentine weekly for 3 months

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: A healthcare worker with a positive T-spot test but negative chest X-ray is prescribed a once-weekly preventive regimen. This protocol consists of [___].
back:
• Isoniazid + Rifapentine
• Dosed once weekly for 3 months (12 doses total)
• Higher completion rates than 9-month INH

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: In the management of MDR-TB, explain why the WHO prefers the use of later-generation fluoroquinolones such as Levofloxacin or Moxifloxacin.
back:
• High in vitro activity against M. tuberculosis
• Moxifloxacin is the most active
• Lower rates of cross-resistance with first-line agents

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Contrast the management of a standard TB patient with a cavitary lesion and positive cultures at 2 months versus a standard non-cavitary case.
back:
• Non-cavitary: 4-month continuation phase
• Cavitary + Positive at 2m: Prolonged continuation phase (7 months)
• Total duration: 9 months to prevent relapse

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Which supplement must be co-administered with Isoniazid during standard TB protocols to prevent peripheral neuropathy, especially in malnourished or alcoholic patients?
back:
• Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
• Recommended dose: 25–50 mg daily
• INH promotes B6 excretion

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: For the standard 6-month WHO treatment course for pulmonary tuberculosis, the initial 2-month intensive phase includes [___], rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol.
back:
• Isoniazid (INH)
• This 4-drug combination is used to ensure coverage against potentially resistant strains before susceptibility results return.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: A 30-year-old male is diagnosed with smear-positive pulmonary tuberculosis. Following the successful completion of the initial 2-month 4-drug intensive phase, the continuation phase should consist of [___].
back:
• Isoniazid and Rifampin
• Duration: 4 months (18 weeks)
• Total standard treatment: 6 months.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
coreConcept: Mechanism of Pyrazinamide in TB Therapy
front: Explain the pharmacodynamic role of Pyrazinamide within the 2-month intensive phase of tuberculosis treatment.
back:
• Acts as a "sterilizing agent"
• Targets residual intracellular organisms in acidic macrophage lysosomes
• Allows reduction of total therapy duration from 9 months to 6 months.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Contrast the standard continuation phase duration for non-cavitary TB with that for a patient exhibiting cavitation and positive cultures at the 2-month mark.
back:
• Non-cavitary: 4 months (18 weeks)
• Cavitation + Positive culture at 2 months: 7 months (31 weeks)
• Prevents relapse in high-burden patients.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Identify the preferred alternative for latent tuberculosis treatment in a patient who cannot tolerate isoniazid.
back:
• Rifampin
• Dosage: 600 mg daily
• Duration: 4 months.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: In the management of Multidrug-Resistant TB (MDR-TB), the agent [___] is utilized as a novel diarylquinoline that specifically inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase.
back:
• Bedaquiline
• Indication: Laboratory-confirmed pulmonary TB resistant to both isoniazid and rifampin
• Duration: 24 weeks.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: A healthcare worker with a positive TST and negative chest radiograph is prescribed a short-course latent TB regimen. This consists of once-weekly isoniazid and [___].
back:
• Rifapentine
• Duration: 3 months (12 doses total)
• Preferred for high-risk latent TB prophylaxis.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Describe the mechanism by which Linezolid carries out its biological function when used as a second-line agent for MDR-TB.
back:
• Protein synthesis inhibitor
• Binds to 23S ribosomal RNA of the 50S subunit
• Effective against strains resistant to all standard first-line drugs.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Contrast the administrative protocols of Rifampin versus Rifabutin in HIV-infected patients undergoing HAART.
back:
• Rifampin: Potent CYP450 inducer; often reduces antiretroviral (PI/NNRTI) levels significantly
• Rifabutin: Less potent inducer; preferred alternative to allow concomitant HIV therapy.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: What is the recommended duration for isoniazid monotherapy in the treatment of latent tuberculosis?
back:
• 9 months
• Dosage: 300 mg daily (or 900 mg twice weekly)
• Effectively reduces the risk of reactivation to active disease.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Patients receiving Ethambutol therapy for tuberculosis must undergo baseline and monthly clinical monitoring of [___] and [___] to detect early drug toxicity.
back:
• Visual acuity
• Red-green color discrimination
• Required to detect dose-related retrobulbar neuritis
• Risk is significantly increased at doses >15 mg/kg/d.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: A 50-year-old alcoholic male on antitubercular therapy develops symmetric paresthesia in his lower extremities. The physician should prescribe [___] to both treat and monitor for this complication.
back:
• Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
• Prevents Isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy
• Recommended dose: 25–50 mg/d
• Essential for high-risk groups (alcoholics, diabetics, AIDS patients).

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
coreConcept: Biochemical Thresholds for TB Drug Discontinuation
front: Explain the biochemical criteria for discontinuing Isoniazid or Pyrazinamide due to hepatotoxicity in an asymptomatic patient.
back:
• Minor elevations (up to 3-4x normal) are often asymptomatic
• Discontinue if AST/ALT exceeds 5x normal (asymptomatic)
• Discontinue if AST/ALT exceeds 3x normal with clinical symptoms (jaundice, RUQ pain).

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
coreConcept: Differential Significance of Pyrazinamide Side Effects
front: Contrast the clinical significance of monitoring serum uric acid versus liver aminotransferases during Pyrazinamide therapy.
back:
• Hyperuricemia: Occurs uniformly/frequently; usually asymptomatic and does not require treatment cessation.
• Hepatotoxicity: Occurs in 1–5% of patients; constitutes a major toxic effect requiring immediate drug discontinuation.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Identify the primary physiologic parameters that must be monitored periodically in a patient receiving Streptomycin as a second-line TB agent.
back:
• Renal function (Creatinine/BUN)
• Vestibular function (Vertigo and balance)
• Audiometry (High-frequency hearing loss)
• Monitor closely in the elderly to prevent permanent ototoxicity.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: During therapy with the second-line agent Cycloserine, serum monitoring is conducted to maintain peak drug concentrations between [___] mcg/mL.
back:
• 20–35 mcg/mL
• Levels >35 mcg/mL correlate with severe CNS toxicity
• Manifestations include tremors, acute psychosis, and seizures
• Peak concentrations occur 2–4 hours post-dose.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: A patient on a four-drug TB regimen presents with orange-colored urine, sweat, and tears. Identify the drug responsible and the appropriate clinical monitoring response.
back:
• Rifampin
• Clinical Response: Patient reassurance (finding is harmless)
• Warning: Warn patient about permanent staining of soft contact lenses
• No dosage adjustment required.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Describe the specific cardiovascular monitoring required for a patient prescribed Bedaquiline for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis.
back:
• Periodic Electrocardiograms (ECG)
• Monitor for QTc interval prolongation
• Check at baseline and weeks 2, 12, and 24
• Discontinue if significant ventricular arrhythmias or QTc >500 ms occur.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Contrast the laboratory monitoring priorities for Rifabutin versus standard Rifampin therapy.
back:
• Rifabutin: Prioritize CBC for leukopenia and thrombocytopenia; monitor for optic neuritis.
• Rifampin: Prioritize liver function tests (cholestatic jaundice) and renal tests for light-chain proteinuria.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: List three specific patient groups who require mandatory monthly serum aminotransferase monitoring while taking Isoniazid.
back:
• Patients older than 35 years
• Patients with chronic liver disease or daily alcohol use
• Pregnant and postpartum women
• Risk of fatal hepatitis increases with these factors.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis

back:

front: D e f i n e m u lt i d rug-r e s i stant tu b e rculosis (M D R-T B) an d i d e nt i fy th e pr i m ary class of s e con d-l i n e oral ag e nts us e d for m anag e m e nt.

front: Th e WHO-r e comme n d e d short-co u rs e r e g i m e n for lat e nt TB us e s a comb i nat i o n of Is o n i az i d an d [___] a d m i n i st e r e d onc e w e e kly for 12 d o s e s.

front: A pat i e nt wi th a r e c e ntly d i agnos e d pulmo nary i n f i ltrat e an d ac i d-fast bac i ll i i n sp ut u m i s starte d on th e r e g i m e n "H R Z E." I f th e i s o lat e i s later fo u n d s u sc e pt i bl e to H an d R, wh i ch drug sh o u l d b e d i scont i n u e d f i rst?

front: D e scr i b e th e s p e c i f i c cl i n i cal ro l e an d m echan i s m of B e d aq u i l i n e i n th e WHO m anag e m e nt of MDR-TB.

front: Contrast th e us e of R i famp i n v e rs u s R i f a b ut i n i n TB pat i e nts co-i n f e ct e d wi th H I V.
back:
• R i famp i n: Pot e nt C Y P i n d u c e r; d e cr e as e s l e v e ls of prot e as e i n h i b i tors
• R i f a b ut i n: L e ss pot e nt i n d u c e r; pr e f e rr e d alternative for pat i e nts on antiretroviral therapy.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: I d e nt i fy th e m an d atory b as e l i n e an d monthly cl i n i cal monitor i ng r e q u i r e d specifically for pat i e nts r e c e i v i ng Etha m b utol.
back:
• V i s u al ac u i ty t e st i ng
• R e d-gr e e n color d i scr i m i nat i o n
• R e as o n: R i sk of d o s e-r e lat e d r e tro b u l b ar n e u r i t i s.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: To prevent peripheral neuropathy during isoniazid (INH) therapy, particularly in malnourished or diabetic patients, the standard supplement is [___].
back:
• Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
• INH promotes B6 excretion
• Essential for patients with alcoholism, pregnancy, or HIV

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
