front: A 50-year-old male on Rifampin, Isoniazid, and Pyrazinamide develops nausea and tea-colored urine. Serum AST is 250 U/L (ULN: 40 U/L). Explain the immediate clinical management regarding drug therapy.
back:
• Discontinue all hepatotoxic drugs (INH, RIF, PZA) immediately
• Drug-induced hepatitis threshold reached (AST >5x ULN asymptomatic, or >3x ULN with symptoms)
• Reintroduce drugs one-by-one after AST returns to <2x ULN

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Explain the role of monthly ophthalmologic assessments for a patient prescribed Ethambutol (EMB) in the intensive phase.
back:
• Monitors for dose-dependent retrobulbar neuritis
• Checks visual acuity (Snellen chart) and red-green color discrimination
• Essential to prevent irreversible vision loss

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: A patient with MDR-TB is treated with Streptomycin. Contrast the physical signs used to monitor for vestibular versus auditory toxicity.
back:
• Vestibular: Ataxia, vertigo, or loss of balance (often irreversible)
• Auditory: Tinnitus and high-frequency hearing loss (monitored via audiometry)

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: State the standard frequency for laboratory monitoring of liver enzymes in an asymptomatic patient without preexisting liver disease taking INH and Rifampin.
back:
• Baseline LFTs (AST/ALT/Bilirubin) required
• Routine monthly testing not mandatory for asymptomatic, low-risk patients
• Repeat only if clinical symptoms (jaundice, anorexia, nausea) appear

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Patients initiating Pyrazinamide (PZA) should be monitored for clinical signs of [___] due to the drug's effect on renal uric acid clearance.
back:
• Hyperuricemia (Gouty arthritis)
• PZA inhibits uric acid excretion
• Monitor for joint pain, swelling, and redness

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: A cardiac patient stabilized on Warfarin starts therapy with Rifampin. Describe the physiological monitoring required for the anticoagulant dose.
back:
• Monitor INR more frequently
• Rifampin is a potent CYP450 inducer (1A2, 2C9, 3A4)
• Warfarin dose usually needs to be increased due to accelerated metabolism

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Identify the visual defect characteristic of Ethambutol toxicity and the specific baseline testing method used.
back:
• Retrobulbar/Optic Neuritis
• Assessed via Ishihara Plates for red-green color blindness
• EMB interferes with mycobacterial cell wall polymerization (arabinosyl transferase)

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Contrast the clinical significance of orange urine versus tea-colored urine in a patient on a standard four-drug TB regimen.
back:
• Orange urine: Harmless Rifampin byproduct; no intervention required
• Tea-colored urine: Sign of hepatotoxicity (bilirubinuria); requires urgent LFT assessment

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Name the three primary first-line antituberculosis agents that contribute to potential hepatotoxicity and require LFT surveillance.
back:
• Isoniazid (INH)
• Rifampin (RIF)
• Pyrazinamide (PZA) - often considered the most hepatotoxic

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: The intensive phase of the standard WHO 6-month regimen for newly diagnosed, drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis lasts for exactly [___] months.
back:
2 months.
- Followed by a 4-month continuation phase.
- The intensive phase includes all four first-line drugs (INH, RIF, PZA, EMB).

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: A patient with a positive tuberculin skin test but no clinical or radiographic signs of active disease is diagnosed with latent tuberculosis. Identify the standard 4-month monotherapy regimen preferred for this condition.
back:
- Rifampin (600 mg) administered daily for 4 months.
- Alternative: Isoniazid monotherapy for 9 months.
- Short course: Weekly Isoniazid plus Rifapentine for 3 months (12 doses).

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Explain the pharmacological rationale for including Pyrazinamide specifically during the first two months of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis treatment.
back:
- Acts as a 'sterilizing agent' against semi-dormant intracellular bacilli.
- It is uniquely active in the acidic environment of macrophage lysosomes.
- Its inclusion allows shortening total therapy from 9 to 6 months.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Contrast the drug components used in the intensive phase versus the continuation phase for standard 6-month drug-susceptible tuberculosis therapy.
back:
- Intensive Phase: Isoniazid, Rifampin, Pyrazinamide, and Ethambutol.
- Continuation Phase: Isoniazid and Rifampin only.
- Purpose: Intensive phase kills actively dividing bacteria; continuation phase targets residual organisms.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Identify the specific drug resistance criteria required to classify Mycobacterium tuberculosis as "Multidrug-Resistant" (MDR-TB).
back:
- Resistance to both Isoniazid and Rifampin.
- Management requires second-line agents (e.g., Bedaquiline, Fluoroquinolones, or Capreomycin).
- Treatment duration is significantly longer, typically 18–24 months.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
coreConcept: Role of Ethambutol in TB Regimens
front: In the standard WHO protocol for pulmonary TB, Ethambutol is primarily added to the initial regimen to protect against potential resistance to [___].
back:
Isoniazid.
- Ethambutol provides additional coverage if the isolate is resistant to INH or RIF.
- It can be discontinued once susceptibility to INH and RIF is confirmed.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: A 30-year-old nurse is found to have a TST conversion. Identify the CDC/WHO-recommended short-course combination regimen that utilizes once-weekly dosing for 12 weeks to manage latent infection.
back:
- Weekly Isoniazid (900 mg) plus Rifapentine (900 mg).
- Total duration: 3 months.
- Efficacy is equivalent to 9 months of Isoniazid monotherapy with better compliance.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Explain why the WHO strictly recommends at least two active agents for pulmonary tuberculosis, whereas monotherapy is acceptable for latent infection.
back:
- Active TB has a high bacterial burden (~10^8 bacilli) containing naturally occurring resistant mutants.
- Monotherapy selects for these mutants, causing treatment failure.
- Latent TB has low bacterial numbers, making resistance selection highly improbable.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Contrast the treatment approach for drug-susceptible TB with MDR-TB regarding the choice of pharmacological classes.
back:
- Drug-Susceptible: Uses first-line oral agents (RIPE: Rifampin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol).
- MDR-TB: Uses second-line agents (e.g., Levofloxacin/Moxifloxacin, Bedaquiline, Linezolid, or injectable Capreomycin/Amikacin).

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: List the four primary first-line medications (the "RIPE" acronym) used in the WHO standard protocol for newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis.
back:
- Rifampin
- Isoniazid
- Pyrazinamide
- Ethambutol
- These form the core of initial therapy to maximize bactericidal and sterilizing activity.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Isoniazid (INH) exerts its primary bactericidal effect against actively growing tubercle bacilli by inhibiting the synthesis of [___], which are vital components of the mycobacterial cell wall.
back:
● Mycolic Acids
● It targets the enzymes AcpM and KasA after activation by the viral catalase-peroxidase KatG
● Disruption leads to loss of cell wall integrity and cell death.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: A patient's sputum culture identifies M. tuberculosis that is resistant to both Isoniazid and Rifampin. Explain the pathophysiology behind the development of this specific resistance profile.
back:
● Categorized as Multidrug-Resistant TB (MDR-TB)
● Result of sequential point mutations (e.g., rpoB for Rifampin, katG for Isoniazid)
● Often caused by poor adherence or improper monotherapy.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Explain how the activity of Pyrazinamide (PZA) distinguishes it as a 'sterilizing agent' compared to other first-line drugs like Isoniazid.
back:
● PZA is active in acidic environments (pH 5.5)
● Targets semi-dormant intracellular bacilli within macrophage lysosomes
● Allows shortening of total treatment from 9 to 6 months.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: A patient with cavitary lung disease completes 2 months of HRZE but remains culture-positive. Contrast the management strategy of the 'Continuation Phase' for this high-risk patient versus a standard non-cavitary case.
back:
● High-risk: Prolong continuation phase to 7 months (total 9 months)
● Standard: Continue for 4 months (total 6 months)
● High-risk requires Rifampin/Isoniazid daily or 3x/weekly.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Identify the critical pharmacological step required before Ethambutol can be safely prescribed to a pediatric patient and the specific adverse effect it aims to monitor.
back:
● Baseline visual acuity and red-green color discrimination testing
● Monitoring for dose-related retrobulbar neuritis
● Avoid in children too young for reliable subjective visual assessment.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: The standard WHO-recommended treatment duration for latent tuberculosis using Isoniazid monotherapy is [___] months, whereas Rifampin monotherapy is typically given for [___] months.
back:
● Isoniazid: 9 months
● Rifampin: 4 months
● Alternatives include weekly Isoniazid + Rifapentine for 3 months.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: An HIV-positive patient on an Efavirenz-based antiretroviral regimen is diagnosed with TB. Describe the necessary adjustment for Rifabutin if used as a Rifampin substitute and the rationale.
back:
● Increase Rifabutin dose to 600 mg daily
● Efavirenz is a CYP3A4 inducer that lowers Rifabutin levels
● Rifabutin is preferred over Rifampin due to less potent induction of PI/NNRTI metabolism.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Explain the biochemical mechanism of Bedaquiline and why it is reserved strictly for cases of MDR-TB or XDR-TB.
back:
● Inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase
● Kills both replicating and non-replicating bacilli
● Reserved due to risks of QTc prolongation, hepatotoxicity, and increased mortality.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Contrast the metabolic elimination and dosing requirements of Pyrazinamide in a patient with a creatinine clearance of 20 mL/min compared to normal renal function.
back:
● Normal: 25 mg/kg daily
● Impaired: 25-35 mg/kg administered 3 times weekly
● Rationale: Metabolites are renally cleared and accumulate in failure.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Identify the nutritional supplement routinely co-administered with Isoniazid in high-risk patients and the specific biochemical reason for its use.
back:
● Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
● Isoniazid forms complexes with pyridoxine, promoting its renal excretion
● Deficiency results in sensory peripheral neuropathy.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: The standard intensive phase for newly diagnosed, drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis lasts [___] months and requires a four-drug combination.
back:
• 2 months.
• Includes Isoniazid, Rifampin, Pyrazinamide, and Ethambutol (HRZE).
• Designed to rapidly kill actively dividing bacilli and prevent the selection of drug-resistant mutants early in therapy.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: A 45-year-old immigrant presents with weight loss, night sweats, and apical cavitary lung lesions. Sputum smear is positive for acid-fast bacilli. The standard WHO-recommended treatment strategy is [___].
back:
• 6-month regimen (2HRZE / 4HR).
• Intensive Phase: 2 months of HRZE.
• Continuation Phase: 4 months of HR (Isoniazid and Rifampin).
• This protocol cures 95–98% of cases caused by susceptible strains.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
coreConcept: Role of Pyrazinamide in TB Therapy
front: Explain the pharmacological rationale for including Pyrazinamide specifically during the first two months of tuberculosis therapy.
back:
• Acts as a "sterilizing agent" against persistent intracellular organisms.
• Highly active in the acidic environment of macrophage lysosomes.
• Its use allow the total treatment duration to be reduced from 9 to 6 months.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Contrast the drug resistance profile defining Multidrug-Resistant TB (MDR-TB) with that of standard drug-susceptible TB.
back:
• MDR-TB: Resistance to at least Isoniazid and Rifampin simultaneously.
• Susceptible TB: Responds to all four first-line agents.
• MDR-TB requires longer treatment (up to 24 months) with more toxic second-line agents.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Identify the standard duration and primary drug used in the traditional monotherapy regimen for latent tuberculosis infection.
back:
• Isoniazid for 6 to 9 months.
• Alternative: Rifampin daily for 4 months.
• Newer option: Isoniazid plus Rifapentine once weekly for 3 months administered via directly observed therapy (DOT).

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: [___] is a diarylquinoline that inhibits mycobacterial ATP synthase and is specifically indicated for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis when other options are exhausted.
back:
• Bedaquiline.
• First drug with a novel mechanism against TB approved in decades.
• Used for 24 weeks in combination with other active drugs for laboratory-confirmed MDR-TB.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: A 25-year-old with a positive TST and negative chest X-ray is diagnosed with latent TB. The preferred short-course regimen to replace 9 months of Isoniazid is [___].
back:
• Isoniazid and Rifapentine once weekly for 3 months (12 doses).
• Another alternative is Rifampin daily for 4 months.
• These shorter regimens improve patient adherence compared to traditional 9-month Isoniazid monotherapy.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Explain the rationale for starting treatment with a four-drug regimen (HRZE) rather than a two-drug regimen before susceptibility results return.
back:
• Protects against existing resistance to single drugs (e.g., Isoniazid resistance prevalence ~10%).
• Prevents emergence of further resistance during treatment.
• Statistical probability of a bacillus being resistant to two drugs simultaneously is extremely low.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
coreConcept: TB Intensive vs. Continuation Phase Goals
front: Contrast the T-tubule triad of skeletal muscle with the diad system of cardiac muscle. (Note: Topic focus requires contrast between TB treatment phases). Contrast the primary goal of the TB intensive phase versus the continuation phase.
back:
• Intensive Phase (2 months): Rapidly reduces total bacterial load and prevents resistance emergence.
• Continuation Phase (4 months): Eliminates semi-dormant "persister" organisms to prevent clinical relapse and achieve long-term cure.

category: Describe standard protocols (WHO recommendation) for management of newly diagnosed pulmonary tuberculosis, multidrug-resistant tuberculosis, latent tuberculosis
front: Identify the class of oral antibiotics now considered a core component of WHO-recommended multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) regimens.
back:
• Fluoroquinolones.
• Specifically Levofloxacin or Moxifloxacin.
• Preferred due to high potency against M. tuberculosis and better tolerability compared to older second-line injectable agents like Capreomycin.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Patients receiving Ethambutol as part of their antituberculosis regimen should undergo baseline and monthly assessments of [___].
back:
• Visual acuity
• Red-green color discrimination
• Purpose: Early detection of dose-related retrobulbar optic neuritis.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: A 45-year-old male on quadruple TB therapy for 2 months presents with numbness and tingling in his feet. This clinical finding indicates toxicity of [___].
back:
• Isoniazid (INH)
• Pathophysiology: Competitive inhibition and increased excretion of Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
• Management: Assess sensory symptoms monthly.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Explain the threshold for liver aminotransferase elevation that necessitates the suspension of hepatotoxic antituberculosis drugs (INH, RIF, PZA).
back:
• Discontinue if ALT/AST >3x normal WITH symptoms (nausea, jaundice, abdominal pain)
• Discontinue if ALT/AST >5x normal WITHOUT symptoms.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Contrast the primary physiologic monitoring requirements for Streptomycin with those for Ethambutol.
back:
• Streptomycin: Periodic audiometry/vestibular testing (Ototoxicity) and BUN/Creatinine (Nephrotoxicity)
• Ethambutol: Monthly ophthalmologic exams for visual acuity and color vision (Optic Neuritis).

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Identify the primary metabolic marker to monitor in a patient receiving Pyrazinamide who develops acute joint pain.
back:
• Serum Uric Acid
• Pyrazinamide inhibits uric acid excretion, causing hyperuricemia
• Monitor for clinical signs of gouty arthritis.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: The gold-standard laboratory marker used to monitor the microbiologic response to therapy in pulmonary tuberculosis is [___].
back:
• Monthly sputum smear and culture
• Conversion to negative usually occurs within 2 months
• Two consecutive negative cultures define therapeutic success.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: A patient on TB therapy is alarmed by orange-red discoloration of his urine and tears. Which drug is responsible and how should the clinician respond?
back:
• Rifampin (or other Rifamycins)
• Harmless side effect; no treatment change required
• Caution patient regarding permanent staining of soft contact lenses.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Describe the physiological basis for monitoring the efficacy of concurrent medications (e.g., Warfarin, OCPs) in patients starting Rifampin.
back:
• Mechanism: Potent induction of hepatic CYP450 isoforms (3A4, 2C9)
• Effect: Accelerates metabolism and reduces serum levels of concurrent drugs
• Monitoring: Check PT/INR or adjust to non-hormonal contraception.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Contrast the monitoring risks for Isoniazid between fast and slow acetylators.
back:
• Slow Acetylators: Higher drug levels; increased risk of peripheral neuropathy and liver damage
• Fast Acetylators: Lower drug levels; increased risk of treatment failure or relapse
• Basis: Genetically determined N-acetyltransferase activity.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: What specific biochemical supplement must be provided and monitored for adherence in TB patients with diabetes or alcoholism on INH therapy?
back:
• Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
• Prevents INH-induced peripheral neuropathy
• INH promotes pyridoxine excretion, especially in high-risk patients.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: To prevent peripheral neuropathy in high-risk patients during isoniazid (INH) therapy, the physician must co-prescribe [___].
back:
● Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6).
● INH promotes B6 excretion by inhibiting its synthesis.
● Critical in patients with alcoholism, diabetes, or malnutrition.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: A 45-year-old male on anti-TB therapy reports difficulty distinguishing traffic light colors. This medication adverse effect requires monthly [___] monitoring.
back:
● Visual acuity and red-green color discrimination testing.
● Ethambutol causes dose-dependent retrobulbar neuritis.
● Early detection prevents permanent optic nerve damage.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Explain the role of clinical counseling regarding orange-colored bodily secretions (urine, tears, sweat) during Rifampin therapy.
back:
● Harmless metabolic side effect of the drug.
● Counseling prevents alarm and improves adherence.
● Patient must avoid soft contact lenses due to permanent staining.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Contrast the primary laboratory monitoring parameters for Pyrazinamide therapy versus Ethambutol therapy.
back:
● Pyrazinamide: Liver enzymes (hepatotoxicity) and serum uric acid (hyperuricemia).
● Ethambutol: Visual testing; no routine laboratory blood monitoring required.
● Both are cleared differently (PZA hepatically; EMB renally).

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Identify the hepatotoxic monitoring threshold requiring immediate discontinuation of Isoniazid (INH).
back:
● Aminotransferases >3x upper limit with symptoms (nausea/jaundice).
● Aminotransferases >5x upper limit in asymptomatic patients.
● Routine monitoring is essential for rapid acetylators and elderly.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: While taking [___], patients are monitored for asymptomatic hyperuricemia, though therapy is usually continued unless clinical gout develops.
back:
● Pyrazinamide (PZA).
● PZA inhibits renal uric acid excretion.
● Monitoring helps distinguish PZA effects from other joint pathologies.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: An HIV-positive patient on protease inhibitors shows a sudden drop in antiretroviral efficacy after starting TB treatment. This indicates a need to monitor [___] induction.
back:
● Cytochrome P450 (CYP3A4) system induction by Rifampin.
● Rifampin significantly lowers serum protease inhibitor levels.
● Monitoring viral load or switching to Rifabutin is required.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Describe the necessary clinical monitoring for a patient receiving Streptomycin as part of a second-line TB regimen.
back:
● Periodic audiometry and vestibular function assessment.
● Renal function (serum creatinine) monitoring.
● Prevents irreversible ototoxicity and acute nephrotoxicity.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Contrast the baseline clinical evaluations essential for initiating Isoniazid versus Ethambutol.
back:
● Isoniazid: Baseline liver function tests (LFTs).
● Ethambutol: Baseline visual acuity and color vision exam.
● Crucial for identifying pre-existing conditions or later drug toxicity.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: List the CNS symptoms that must be monitored in a patient receiving Cycloserine for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis.
back:
● Tremors, headaches, acute psychosis, and convulsions.
● Dose-related neurotoxicity; avoid concentrations >35 mcg/mL.
● High-dose pyridoxine supplementation helps minimize these effects.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: [FILL_IN_THE_BLANK] During therapy with Ethambutol, patients must undergo baseline and monthly objective testing for [___] to detect retrobulbar neuritis.
back:
• Visual acuity
• Red-green color discrimination
• Monitoring is critical because toxicity is dose-dependent and typically occurs after at least one month of treatment.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: [CLINICAL_SCENARIO] An asymptomatic TB patient on Isoniazid shows a three-fold rise in serum aminotransferases. Explain the appropriate clinical monitoring and management for this finding.
back:
• Continue therapy with close observation.
• Minor elevations (up to 3-4x normal) occur in 10-20% and are usually asymptomatic.
• Discontinue drug immediately if symptomatic hepatitis develops.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: [MECHANISM_EXPLANATION] Describe the significance of monitoring serum uric acid levels in patients during Pyrazinamide therapy.
back:
• Pyrazinamide uniformly causes hyperuricemia.
• It inhibits renal urate excretion.
• Asymptomatic hyperuricemia is common; monitoring is primarily to assess the risk of clinical gouty arthritis.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: [DIFFERENTIAL_CONTRAST] Contrast the primary physiological system monitoring requirements for a patient receiving Streptomycin versus one receiving Ethambutol.
back:
• Streptomycin: Requires auditory/vestibular assessments (ototoxicity) and BUN/creatinine (nephrotoxicity).
• Ethambutol: Requires ophthalmologic assessments (optic neuritis).
• Streptomycin monitoring is frequent in the elderly and renal-impaired.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: [DIRECT_CONCEPT] Identify the essential cardiac monitoring step required for patients initiated on Bedaquiline therapy.
back:
• Baseline and periodic Electrocardiogram (ECG).
• Purpose: Detect QTc interval prolongation (Black-box warning).
• Risk is increased if co-administered with other QT-prolonging agents.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: [FILL_IN_THE_BLANK] Patients initiated on Rifampin should be monitored for psychological distress regarding discoloration and counseled that their [___] may turn a harmless orange-red color.
back:
• Urine, sweat, and tears.
• Harmless orange pigmentation is a signature effect of all rifamycins.
• Patients should be warned that soft contact lenses may be permanently stained.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: [CLINICAL_SCENARIO] A patient receiving Cycloserine for multidrug-resistant TB develops tremors and depression. Explain the monitoring strategy used to prevent these central nervous system toxicities.
back:
• Monitor peak serum concentrations (Goal: 20-35 mcg/mL).
• Toxicity is dose-related; risks increase when peak levels exceed 35 mcg/mL.
• Co-administer Pyridoxine (≥100 mg/day) to ameliorate neurologic effects.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: [MECHANISM_EXPLANATION] Explain the rationale for weekly Complete Blood Count (CBC) monitoring in patients receiving Linezolid for tuberculosis.
back:
• Detect bone marrow suppression (especially thrombocytopenia).
• Toxicity is duration-dependent, typically occurring after 2 weeks of use.
• Monitor to prevent irreversible peripheral and optic neuropathy seen in prolonged courses.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: [DIFFERENTIAL_CONTRAST] Contrast the drug-interaction monitoring concerns for HIV-infected patients taking Rifampin versus Rifabutin regarding antiretroviral therapy (ART).
back:
• Rifampin: Potent inducer of multiple CYP450 isoforms; monitor for ART failure due to subtherapeutic drug levels.
• Rifabutin: Less potent inducer; used when PIs are required.
• Rifabutin doses require adjustment based on the specific ART agent.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: [DIRECT_CONCEPT] Identify the specific symptoms that warrant immediate serum monitoring or clinical intervention to prevent permanent injury in patients on Isoniazid.
back:
• Paresthesias (numbness/tingling) in the hands and feet.
• Suggests peripheral neuropathy from drug-induced pyridoxine deficiency.
• High-risk groups (alcoholics, diabetics, malnourished) require prophylactic pyridoxine monitoring.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Patients receiving Ethambutol as part of their antituberculosis regimen should undergo baseline and monthly monitoring of [___] and red-green color discrimination.
back:
● Visual acuity.
● Reason: To detect dose-related retrobulbar neuritis early.
● Management: This side effect is usually reversible if the drug is discontinued promptly.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: [CLINICAL_SCENARIO] A 45-year-old male on TB therapy presents with tingling and numbness in his feet. Laboratory tests show normal liver enzymes. The most likely cause is a deficiency of [___] induced by Isoniazid.
back:
● Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6).
● Pathophysiology: INH promotes the excretion of B6, leading to peripheral neuropathy.
● Prevention: Co-administer 25–50 mg of pyridoxine daily in high-risk patients (alcoholics, diabetics).

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: [MECHANISM_EXPLANATION] Explain the clinical significance of monitoring serum uric acid levels in a patient receiving Pyrazinamide.
back:
● Pyrazinamide inhibits renal uric acid excretion.
● Result: Hyperuricemia occurs in nearly all patients.
● Clinical Note: Asymptomatic hyperuricemia is usually not an indication to stop therapy; monitor for clinical gout.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: [DIFFERENTIAL_CONTRAST] Contrast the management approach to asymptomatic aminotransferase elevations versus clinical jaundice in a patient on Isoniazid therapy.
back:
● Asymptomatic (<3-4x normal): Continue therapy with close observation; often resolves spontaneously.
● Clinical Jaundice: Immediate, permanent discontinuation required.
● Risk: Failure to stop can lead to fatal hepatic necrosis.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: [DIRECT_CONCEPT] Identify the pharmacological reason why Rifampin necessitates the monitoring of concurrent medications like methadone or oral contraceptives.
back:
● Potent induction of Cytochrome P450 isoforms (3A4, 2C9, 2C19).
● Effect: Drastically increases the elimination of co-administered drugs.
● Consequence: Leads to subtherapeutic levels and potential treatment failure of the secondary medication.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: In the monitoring of pulmonary tuberculosis therapy, a successful response to the intensive phase is primarily indicated by [___] conversion during the first two months.
back:
● Sputum culture (or smear).
● Importance: Failure to convert suggests potential drug resistance or non-compliance.
● Action: If positive at 2 months, the continuation phase may need extension.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: [CLINICAL_SCENARIO] A patient being treated for TB notices his urine, sweat, and tears have turned orange-red. This finding indicates the need for [___].
back:
● Patient reassurance only.
● Causative Drug: Rifampin.
● Clinical Fact: This is a harmless side effect; patients should be warned beforehand to avoid unnecessary alarm.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
coreConcept: TB Drug Adjustment in Renal Failure
front: [MECHANISM_EXPLANATION] Describe the specific dosing modification required for a patient with a creatinine clearance < 30 mL/min receiving Ethambutol or Pyrazinamide.
back:
● Frequency reduction: Change from daily to three times weekly.
● Rationale: Prevents accumulation of the parent drug or toxic metabolites.
● Goal: Minimizes risk of dose-related ocular and systemic toxicity.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: [DIFFERENTIAL_CONTRAST] Distinguish between the monitoring requirements for Rifampin versus Rifabutin when used in an HIV-infected patient on protease inhibitors.
back:
● Rifampin: Usually avoided; contraindicated with most protease inhibitors due to extreme enzyme induction.
● Rifabutin: Preferred alternative; less potent inducer.
● Monitoring: Requires Rifabutin dose reduction (to 150mg) to prevent toxicity from inhibited metabolism.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: [DIRECT_CONCEPT] Identify the essential baseline laboratory tests required before starting the standard four-drug RIPE antituberculosis regimen.
back:
● Liver Function Tests (Aminotransferases, Bilirubin).
● Renal Function (Serum Creatinine).
● Uric Acid.
● Baseline Vision Screen (Acuity and Color).

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Monthly monitoring of [___] is standard clinical practice for patients on ethambutol to detect early signs of retrobulbar neuritis.
back: * Visual acuity and red-green color discrimination. * Necessary to detect early dose-related optic toxicity. * Particularly critical if the dosage exceeds 15 mg/kg/d.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: A 52-year-old male on RIPE therapy develops anorexia and jaundice with an AST of 400 U/L (baseline 30). Identify the diagnosis and immediate clinical step.
back: * Drug-induced hepatitis (INH, RIF, or PZA). * Discontinue all hepatotoxic medications immediately. * Re-challenge only after enzymes return to less than twice baseline.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Explain the role of clinical screening for eighth cranial nerve function in patients receiving aminoglycosides for multi-drug resistant TB.
back: * Monitors for irreversible ototoxicity and vestibular damage. * Includes testing for hearing loss (tinnitus) and vertigo (ataxia). * Requires baseline and periodic audiometry assessments.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Contrast the monitoring criteria for continuing versus stopping TB therapy in an asymptomatic patient with elevated liver enzymes.
back: * Continue: Asymptomatic and AST elevation <3-5 times normal. * Discontinue: Clinical symptoms of hepatitis or AST elevation >5 times normal. * Common with INH, RIF, and PZA.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Identify the specific microbiological parameter assessed at 2 months to determine the success of the intensive phase of tuberculosis treatment.
back: * Sputum smear and culture conversion to negative. * Persistent positive cultures suggest treatment failure or drug resistance. * conversion failure necessitates an extension of the continuation phase.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: To monitor for musculoskeletal complications of Pyrazinamide therapy, clinicians should periodically assess serum [___] levels.
back: * Uric acid levels. * Pyrazinamide inhibits uric acid excretion. * Can cause asymptomatic hyperuricemia or provoke acute gouty arthritis.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: A patient on Isoniazid develops distal numbness and paresthesias. Identify the necessary laboratory investigation or supplement required to resolve this finding.
back: * Clinical diagnosis of peripheral neuropathy. * Requires Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) supplementation. * Caused by INH-induced pyridoxine excretion, especially in slow acetylators.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Describe the physiological monitoring required to prevent permanent renal damage in patients receiving second-line injectable TB drugs.
back: * Regular serum creatinine and BUN monitoring. * Streptomycin, Amikacin, and Capreomycin are nephrotoxic. * Dose adjustments are mandatory if calculated creatinine clearance falls below 30-50 mL/min.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Contrast the monitoring protocol for a patient with cavitary disease versus non-cavitary disease during the continuation phase.
back: * Cavitary disease: Requires extension of the continuation phase to 7 months if 2-month cultures are positive. * Non-cavitary disease: Standard 4-month continuation phase if clinical progress is adequate.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Identify the hematological monitoring required for patients receiving prolonged therapy with Rifabutin or Linezolid for drug-resistant TB.
back: * Complete blood count (CBC) with differential. * Monitor for leukopenia, thrombocytopenia (Rifabutin), or bone marrow suppression (Linezolid). * Linezolid toxicity is highly duration-dependent.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: To prevent peripheral neuropathy in patients with predisposing conditions receiving isoniazid, the clinician should co-administer [___].
back:
* Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
* Counteracts the INH-promoted excretion of pyridoxine
* Particularly essential for patients at higher risk, such as those with diabetes, alcoholism, or malnutrition.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: A 45-year-old male on a standard four-drug anti-TB regimen reports difficulty distinguishing traffic light colors. This symptom is most likely due to toxicity of which drug, and what specific baseline test should have been performed?
back:
* Drug: Ethambutol
* Pathology: Dose-related retrobulbar neuritis
* Monitoring: Baseline and monthly visual acuity and red-green color discrimination testing.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Explain the difference in management between a patient with asymptomatic minor increases in liver aminotransferases and one with clinical jaundice during isoniazid therapy.
back:
* Asymptomatic (<3-4x normal): Therapy usually continues with close observation
* Clinical Jaundice: Requires immediate, permanent drug discontinuation
* Hepatitis risk increases significantly with age over 35.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Contrast the monitoring requirements for an HIV-infected patient on protease inhibitors receiving Rifampin versus one switched to Rifabutin.
back:
* Rifampin: Potent CYP3A4 inducer; monitor for HIV treatment failure due to subtherapeutic PI levels
* Rifabutin: Less potent inducer; monitor for leukopenia and uveitis while adjusting PI doses.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Identify the pharmacological step required when a patient on pyrazinamide develops asymptomatic elevated serum uric acid levels.
back:
* No step/change required; hyperuricemia occurs uniformly with PZA
* Action: Continue therapy unless signs of acute gouty arthritis or renal dysfunction appear.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Patients receiving injectable streptomycin as part of multidrug-resistant TB therapy should undergo periodic monitoring of [___] and renal function.
back:
* Vestibular and auditory function (ototoxicity)
* Toxicity is dose-related and more frequent in elderly patients
* Hearing loss may be permanent.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: A patient 4 weeks into TB therapy develops right upper quadrant pain and anorexia. Identify the three first-line drugs most likely responsible and the clinical threshold for discontinuation.
back:
* Drugs: Isoniazid (INH), Rifampin (RIF), and Pyrazinamide (PZA)
* Threshold: Discontinue if aminotransferases exceed 3x normal with symptoms (or 5x normal without symptoms).

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Describe the clinical management for a patient who develops a 'flu-like syndrome' characterized by fever and chills specifically while on an intermittent rifampin regimen.
back:
* Management: Switch from intermittent to daily dosing
* Mechanism: Hypersensitivity reaction associated with less than twice-weekly dosing
* Monitoring: Screen for accompanying acute tubular necrosis or thrombocytopenia.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Contrast the primary clinical risks between 'rapid acetylators' and 'slow acetylators' receiving intermittent isoniazid therapy.
back:
* Rapid Acetylators: Higher risk of subtherapeutic drug levels and therapeutic failure
* Slow Acetylators: Higher risk of dose-dependent peripheral neuropathy and hepatotoxicity.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Name the specific harmless side effect of Rifampin that causes discoloration of bodily secretions.
back:
* Orange discoloration of urine, sweat, and tears
* Mechanism: Natural color of the drug and metabolites
* Note: Warn patients that soft contact lenses may be permanently stained.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Patients receiving Ethambutol as part of their antituberculosis regimen require monthly assessment of [___] and [___] due to the risk of retrobulbar neuritis.
back:
• Visual acuity
• Red-green color discrimination
• Testing is critical as toxicity is dose-related and may be irreversible if not detected early.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: A 55-year-old patient with a history of alcohol use disorder begins therapy for pulmonary tuberculosis. Two weeks later, he presents with nausea and right upper quadrant pain. Monitoring of [___] is the most immediate laboratory priority.
back:
• Serum aminotransferases (ALT/AST)
• Isoniazid, Rifampin, and Pyrazinamide are all potentially hepatotoxic.
• Discontinuation is required if ALT/AST exceeds 3–5x the upper limit of normal.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Explain the pharmacological rationale for monitoring and potentially adjusting the dosage of methadone or warfarin when starting a Rifampin-based regimen.
back:
• Rifampin is a potent inducer of multiple CYP450 isoforms (3A4, 2C9, 2C19).
• It accelerates the metabolism and clearance of many drugs, leading to subtherapeutic levels and clinical failure.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: [DIFFERENTIAL_CONTRAST] Contrast the primary organ system monitoring required for Streptomycin versus Ethambutol therapy.
back:
• Streptomycin: Auditory/vestibular function (ototoxicity) and renal function (nephrotoxicity).
• Ethambutol: Optic nerve function (retrobulbar neuritis/vision).

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Identify the laboratory parameter that frequently increases during Pyrazinamide therapy but rarely requires drug discontinuation unless the patient becomes symptomatic.
back:
• Serum uric acid (Hyperuricemia)
• Pyrazinamide inhibits urate excretion.
• Only symptomatic gout or severe joint pain typically warrants drug cessation.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: To minimize the risk of fatal cardiac events, patients receiving the second-line agent [___] must be monitored with periodic electrocardiograms (ECGs) to evaluate the [___].
back:
• Bedaquiline
• QTc interval
• This drug carries a Black Box Warning for QTc prolongation and associated mortality.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: A patient being treated for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis develops new-onset tremors, depression, and memory loss. This clinical presentation requires urgent monitoring of [___] serum levels.
back:
• Cycloserine
• Target peak concentrations: 20–35 mcg/mL.
• Supplemental Pyridoxine (100 mg/d) is often used to ameliorate these CNS toxicities.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Describe the physiological mechanism that necessitates frequent renal function monitoring when using injectable Amikacin for tuberculosis.
back:
• Amikacin is cleared exclusively via glomerular filtration.
• Declining GFR leads to drug accumulation.
• High trough levels significantly increase the risk of irreversible ototoxicity and further nephrotoxicity.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: [DIFFERENTIAL_CONTRAST] Distinguish the clinical significance of orange-colored sweat/urine versus scleral icterus in a patient on RIPE therapy.
back:
• Orange fluids: Expected, harmless effect of Rifampin.
• Scleral icterus: Sign of clinical hepatitis/hyperbilirubinemia (toxicity).
• Requires immediate liver function testing and potential drug interruption.

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Why is it standard practice to monitor for paresthesias and administer Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) to patients receiving Isoniazid (INH)?
back:
• INH promotes Pyridoxine excretion.
• Deficiency leads to peripheral neuropathy and CNS dysfunction.
• High-risk groups (alcoholics, diabetics, malnourished) require mandatory daily supplementation.

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: The second-line antitubercular agent that acts by inhibiting mycobacterial ATP synthase is [___].
back:
• Bedaquiline
• Therapeutic: Used for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB)
• Adverse: QTc interval prolongation and hepatotoxicity
• Note: Administer with a high-fat meal to increase absorption

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: A patient on an MDR-TB regimen presents with depression, tremors, and acute psychosis. These neuropsychiatric symptoms are most likely caused by [___].
back:
• Cycloserine
• Therapeutic: Cell wall synthesis inhibitor (D-alanine analog)
• Adverse: Dose-related CNS toxicity, headaches, and convulsions
• Management: Co-administer pyridoxine (100 mg+) to mitigate neurologic effects

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Explain the mechanism by which Ethionamide exerts its therapeutic effect against M. tuberculosis.
back:
• Chemically related to Isoniazid
• Blocks mycolic acid synthesis
• Acts as a prodrug requiring bacterial activation
• Effective against both intracellular and extracellular bacilli

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Contrast the adverse effect profile of Bedaquiline with that of Linezolid in a patient undergoing long-term therapy for XDR-TB.
back:
• Bedaquiline: QTc prolongation (cardiac monitoring required) and significant hepatotoxicity
• Linezolid: Reversible bone marrow suppression (thrombocytopenia) and potentially irreversible optic/peripheral neuropathy

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Identify the specific injectable second-line drug used in MDR-TB that is a peptide protein synthesis inhibitor rather than an aminoglycoside.
back:
• Capreomycin
• Therapeutic: Inhibits protein synthesis
• Adverse: Nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity (tinnitus, vestibular disturbance)
• Note: Often active against streptomycin-resistant strains

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: To mitigate the peripheral neuropathy and CNS dysfunction associated with Cycloserine or Ethionamide therapy, patients are typically supplemented with [___].
back:
• Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
• Rationale: Ameliorates neurotoxicity by addressing relative B6 deficiency induced by these agents
• Dosage: 100 mg+ daily for Cycloserine; standard doses for Ethionamide

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: A patient being treated for MDR-TB with a regimen including Amikacin and Bedaquiline requires monitoring for [___] and [___] respectively.
back:
• Amikacin: Nephrotoxicity (creatinine) and ototoxicity (audiometry)
• Bedaquiline: Cardiac conduction abnormalities (electrocardiogram for QTc) and liver function tests

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Explain the molecular basis for cross-resistance between the first-line drug Isoniazid and the second-line drug Ethionamide.
back:
• Primary cause: Mutations resulting in overexpression of inhA gene
• Target: inhA encodes NADH-dependent acyl carrier protein reductase
• Result: Both drugs fail to inhibit mycolic acid synthesis

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Distinguish between the primary toxicities of Para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS) and Capreomycin.
back:
• PAS: Severe gastrointestinal irritation, peptic ulceration, and hypersensitivity reactions (fever/joint pain)
• Capreomycin: Renal impairment and eighth nerve damage (ototoxicity/vertigo)

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: List two fluoroquinolones specifically recommended by the WHO as second-line agents for MDR-TB due to their superior activity against M. tuberculosis.
back:
• Moxifloxacin
• Levofloxacin
• Benefit: Faster bactericidal activity compared to other agents
• Caution: Must be used in combination to avoid rapid resistance

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: To prevent ethambutol-induced toxicity, monthly clinical monitoring is focused on the [___], which is the primary anatomic site of drug damage.
back:
* Optic nerve (Retrobulbar neuritis)
* Manifests as decreased visual acuity
* Causes red-green color blindness

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: A patient on antituberculosis therapy develops right upper quadrant pain, jaundice, and anorexia. Identify the most likely drug-induced clinical condition.
back:
* Clinical hepatitis
* Caused by hepatocellular damage (usually INH or PZA)
* Requires permanent drug discontinuation

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Explain the role of Pyridoxine supplementation in the management of patients receiving Isoniazid (INH).
back:
* INH promotes excessive renal excretion of pyridoxine
* Supplementation prevents peripheral neuropathy
* Also prevents CNS toxicities (seizures, psychosis)

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Contrast the clinical significance of drug-induced hyperuricemia from Pyrazinamide with that of retrobulbar neuritis from Ethambutol.
back:
* Hyperuricemia: Common/harmless; continue therapy if asymptomatic
* Retrobulbar neuritis: Serious/potentially permanent; requires immediate drug cessation

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Identify the mandatory cardiac monitoring parameter for a patient initiated on Bedaquiline for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis.
back:
* Electrocardiogram (EKG)
* Specifically monitors for QTc interval prolongation
* Prevents fatal arrhythmias

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: During therapy, patients should be monitored for the harmless side effect of orange-colored secretions caused by the drug [___].
back:
* Rifampin
* Colors urine, sweat, and tears
* May permanently stain soft contact lenses

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: A 65-year-old patient on Streptomycin therapy presents with tinnitus and loss of balance. Identify the specific nerve affected and the necessary monitoring.
back:
* Eighth (VIII) cranial nerve (vestibulotoxicity)
* Requires monitoring of renal function/serum creatinine
* Adjust dosage to prevent drug accumulation

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Describe the physiological target used when monitoring Cycloserine serum levels to minimize central nervous system toxicity.
back:
* Peak concentrations measured 2–4 hours post-dose
* Target range: 20–35 mcg/mL
* Prevents headache, tremors, and acute psychosis

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: Contrast the significance of a two-fold versus a five-fold asymptomatic rise in liver aminotransferases during Isoniazid therapy.
back:
* Two-to-three fold rise: Common/transient; do not stop therapy
* Five-fold asymptomatic rise: Significant; requires evaluation/cessation consideration (UHS standard)

category: Describe how to monitor patients during antituberculosis drug therapy
front: List the laboratory test necessary to monitor for the primary dose-limiting toxicity of Linezolid in tuberculosis therapy.
back:
* Complete Blood Count (CBC)
* Monitors for reversible bone marrow suppression
* Specifically identifies thrombocytopenia and anemia

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: The novel second-line antituberculosis agent Bedaquiline achieves its bactericidal effect by specifically targeting the mycobacterial [___] enzyme.
back:
• ATP synthase.
• Inhibits the proton pump mechanism of the enzyme.
• Disrupts energy production in both replicating and non-replicating bacilli.

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: A patient with MDR-TB develops acute depression, tremors, and a seizure after adding a structural analog of D-alanine to their regimen. Identify the likely drug and its primary toxicity.
back:
• Cycloserine.
• Dose-related CNS toxicity (psychosis, convulsions, headache).
• Ameliorated by co-administration of Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6).

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Explain the biochemical interaction between Ethionamide and the InhA gene product in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
back:
• Inhibits InhA (enoyl-ACP reductase).
• Prevents mycolic acid synthesis (similar to Isoniazid).
• Requires activation by EthA (monooxygenase) within the parasite.

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Contrast the primary ototoxicity risks of second-line aminoglycosides like Amikacin versus the cyclic peptide Capreomycin.
back:
• Amikacin: Primarily auditory damage (hearing loss).
• Capreomycin: Primarily vestibular damage (vertigo, ataxia).
• Both are highly nephrotoxic and require renal dose adjustments.

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Identify the specific hematologic monitoring required for a patient receiving Linezolid for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis.
back:
• Weekly Full Blood Counts.
• Risk of reversible bone marrow suppression (Thrombocytopenia).
• Prolonged use (>2 weeks) increases risk of irreversible optic/peripheral neuropathy.

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: In the management of MDR-TB, Levofloxacin and Moxifloxacin are highly effective because they inhibit the bacterial enzyme [___].
back:
• DNA Gyrase (Topoisomerase II).
• Prevents relaxation of supercoiled DNA required for transcription.
• Also inhibits Topoisomerase IV to block bacterial cell division.

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: A patient on a multi-drug regimen for resistant TB presents with severe epigastric distress and a positive test for light-chain proteinuria. Which agent is most likely responsible?
back:
• Para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS).
• Known for extreme GI intolerance and peptic ulceration.
• Causes hypersensitivity, hepatosplenomegaly, and crystalluria in acidic urine.

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: How does the metabolic pathway of Bedaquiline dictate its primary drug-drug interaction contraindications?
back:
• Metabolized by CYP3A4.
• Avoid strong inhibitors (ketoconazole) or inducers (Rifampin).
• Risks QTc interval prolongation; requires mandatory ECG monitoring.

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Contrast the thyroid-related adverse effects of Ethionamide with those of Para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS).
back:
• Both can cause Hypothyroidism.
• Ethionamide interferes with thyroid hormone synthesis.
• PAS inhibits iodine organification; monitoring TSH is essential.

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: List the most critical side effects and therapeutic uses for Clofazimine in resistant mycobacterial infections.
back:
• Skin discoloration (red-brown to black).
• GI intolerance and abdominal pain.
• Used for MDR-TB and multibacillary leprosy.

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: The second-line antitubercular agent [___] is a structural analog of D-alanine that inhibits cell wall synthesis by blocking alanine racemase and D-alanyl-D-alanine ligase.
back:
● Cycloserine
● Potent against Mycobacterium tuberculosis
● Exerts bacteriostatic action
● High risk of dose-related CNS toxicity

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: A 42-year-old male with MDR-TB develops severe depression, tremors, and acute psychosis two weeks after adding a specific oral agent to his regimen. These symptoms are likely caused by [___].
back:
● Cycloserine
● CNS adverse effects include depression, psychosis, and seizures
● Toxicity is common at doses >0.75 g/day
● Managed with Pyridoxine (100 mg/day)

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Explain the biological mechanism by which Capreomycin inhibits Mycobacterium tuberculosis and its primary route of administration.
back:
● Mechanism: Peptide protein synthesis inhibitor
● Route: Intramuscular (injectable)
● Used for multidrug-resistant strains
● Effective against many streptomycin-resistant isolates

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: A patient with MDR-TB and a creatinine clearance of 25 mL/min requires treatment adjustment. Contrast the renal considerations for Cycloserine and Ethionamide.
back:
● Cycloserine: Primarily renally cleared; dose must be reduced (e.g., 500 mg 3x/week)
● Ethionamide: Hepatically metabolized; no specific renal adjustment required
● Cycloserine accumulates rapidly in renal failure, increasing seizure risk

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Identify the second-line oral agent that acts as a folate synthesis antagonist and is uniquely administered as delayed-release granules sprinkled on acidic food.
back:
● Aminosalicylic Acid (PAS)
● PABA structural analog
● Therapeutic effect: Folate synthesis inhibition
● Adverse effects: Gastrointestinal distress, peptic ulceration, and hypersensitivity

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: To minimize the risk of peripheral neuropathy and CNS dysfunction, patients receiving Cycloserine or Ethionamide should be co-administered [___].
back:
● Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
● Ameliorates neurologic toxicity
● Recommended dose for Cycloserine is 100 mg/day
● Essential for slow acetylators

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: A 50-year-old on MDR-TB therapy presents with a 5.5-month terminal half-life drug regimen. He reports nausea and headache. The drug must be taken with a high-fat meal to ensure [___].
back:
● Bedaquiline absorption (two-fold increase)
● Inhibits ATP synthase
● Highly protein-bound (>99%)
● Long half-life due to slow tissue release

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: How does the administration requirement for Aminosalicylic Acid (PAS) granules differ from typical oral tablets regarding pH environments?
back:
● PAS granules require acidic vehicles (yogurt/juice)
● Protects delayed-release coating integrity
● Prevents premature gastric degradation
● Reduces severe gastrointestinal irritation

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Contrast the clinical utility and primary toxicity profiles of Amikacin and Capreomycin in the context of injectable second-line therapy.
back:
● Utility: Both used for streptomycin-resistant TB
● Toxicity: Both are nephrotoxic and ototoxic
● Capreomycin: Higher risk of sterile abscesses at injection sites
● Amikacin: Preferred for specific MDR-TB susceptibility

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Name the two specific biochemical targets inhibited by Aminosalicylic Acid (PAS) similarity to other antifolates.
back:
● Dihydropteroate synthase
● Folate synthesis pathway
● Mechanism: Competes with p-amino-benzoic acid (PABA)
● Active almost exclusively against M. tuberculosis

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: To mitigate the central nervous system toxicities such as tremors and acute psychosis associated with Cycloserine therapy, patients should receive supplemental [___].
back:
• Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
• Ameliorates neurologic toxicity
• Dosage: Typically 100 mg/d or more
• Recommended if peak levels exceed 35 mcg/mL

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: A patient with MDR-TB on a long-term second-line regimen develops blurred vision and persistent tingling in the feet. Labs show a significant drop in platelet count. Which drug is most likely responsible?
back:
• Linezolid
• Causes optic and peripheral neuropathy
• Results in bone marrow suppression (Thrombocytopenia)
• Due to inhibition of mitochondrial protein synthesis

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Explain the pharmacological mechanism by which Aminosalicylic acid (PAS) inhibits Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
back:
• Folate synthesis antagonist
• Competes with p-amino-benzoic acid (PABA)
• Structurally similar to sulfonamides
• Blocks sequential steps in the folate pathway

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Contrast the cross-resistance patterns between Streptomycin-resistant M. tuberculosis and the second-line injectables Amikacin and Capreomycin.
back:
• Streptomycin-resistant strains are usually susceptible to Amikacin/Capreomycin
• Kanamycin resistance often predicts Amikacin resistance
• Capreomycin resistance may show cross-resistance with Amikacin
• Resistance markers include mutations in rrs, rpsL, or tlyA genes

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Why is the use of Ethionamide frequently limited to daily dosages of 500–750 mg despite a theoretical requirement for 1 g?
back:
• Severe gastric irritation
• Intense nausea and vomiting
• Neurologic symptoms (ameliorated by pyridoxine)
• Hepatotoxicity risk with higher dosing

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Resistance to the second-line injectable Streptomycin primarily results from point mutations in either the [___] gene (encoding S12 protein) or the rrs gene (encoding 16S rRNA).
back:
• rpsL gene
• Alters the ribosomal binding site
• Results in high-level resistance
• Renders the drug unable to inhibit protein synthesis

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: An MDR-TB patient initiated on Bedaquiline requires baseline and regular monitoring of which specific laboratory and diagnostic tests to ensure safety?
back:
• Electrocardiogram (ECG) for QTc prolongation
• Liver function tests (transaminases)
• Monitoring for headache and arthralgia
• Assessment for potential drug interactions via CYP3A4

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Describe the biochemical inhibition sequence of Cycloserine in the synthesis of the mycobacterial cell wall.
back:
• Structural analog of D-alanine
• Inhibits Alanine racemase (L-ala to D-ala conversion)
• Inhibits D-alanyl-D-alanine ligase
• Prevents incorporation of D-alanine into peptidoglycan pentapeptide

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Contrast the administration requirements and gastrointestinal tolerability of PAS delayed-release granules compared to standard older PAS formulations.
back:
• Granules swallowed whole with acidic liquid (juice/yogurt)
• Protects delayed-release coating from premature degradation
• Markedly improved GI tolerability
• Slower, more consistent absorption into systemic circulation

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Which second-line injectable agent is derived from Streptomyces capreolus and is utilized when M. tuberculosis is resistant to streptomycin?
back:
• Capreomycin
• Peptide protein synthesis inhibitor
• Dose-related nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity
• Administered 15 mg/kg/d (max 1 g)

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: To maintain the integrity of its delayed-release coating, the second-line agent Aminosalicylic acid (PAS) must be administered by [___].
back:
- Sprinkling granules over applesauce or yogurt
- Swallowing whole swirled in fruit juice
- Prevents premature gastric degradation and irritation

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: A patient with MDR-TB receiving a multi-drug regimen develops progressive peripheral neuropathy and blurred vision. Which oxazolidinone is most likely responsible?
back:
- Linezolid
- Causes mitochondrial protein synthesis inhibition
- Toxicity increases with treatment duration (>2 weeks)

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Explain how the second-line peptide antibiotic Capreomycin inhibits Mycobacterium tuberculosis replication.
back:
- Inhibits bacterial protein synthesis
- Binds to the 16S ribosomal RNA
- Effective against MDR strains resistant to streptomycin

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Contrast the molecular resistance mechanisms of Streptomycin and Amikacin in the management of multidrug-resistant tuberculosis.
back:
- Streptomycin: Point mutations in rpsL (S12 protein) or rrs genes
- Amikacin: Mutations in rrs, eis, or tlyA
- Amikacin often maintains activity against streptomycin-resistant strains

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Identify the clinical rationale for escalating Ethionamide in 250 mg daily increments rather than initiating full-dose therapy.
back:
- Improves patient tolerability
- Minimizes severe gastric irritation and neurologic symptoms
- Maximum tolerable dose is often 500–750 mg

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Due to its high protein binding and slow release from peripheral tissues, the terminal elimination half-life of Bedaquiline is approximately [___].
back:
- 5.5 months
- Reflects persistence in sequestered tissue reservoirs
- Metabolized primarily via the CYP3A4 system

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: A patient with MDR-TB and a creatinine clearance of 25 mL/min requires Cycloserine. What specific dosage adjustment is mandatory to prevent CNS toxicity?
back:
- Reduce dose by 50% (to 250-500 mg daily)
- Alternatively: 500 mg three times weekly
- Prevents accumulation-induced psychoses and seizures

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Explain the biological mechanism allowing for cross-resistance between Bedaquiline and Clofazimine in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
back:
- Upregulation of the multisubstrate MmpL5 efflux pump
- Increases drug export out of the mycobacterial cell
- Confers resistance despite distinct primary targets

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Contrast Levofloxacin and Moxifloxacin with Ciprofloxacin regarding their clinical utility for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis.
back:
- Levofloxacin/Moxifloxacin: Superior activity against M. tuberculosis (later-generation)
- Ciprofloxacin: Less active; primarily used for atypical mycobacteria
- Moxifloxacin is the most active in vitro

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Which vitamin supplement is used to ameliorate the neurologic toxicities associated with both Cycloserine and Ethionamide?
back:
- Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6)
- Ameliorates peripheral neuropathy and CNS symptoms
- Standard dose is 100 mg/day or more

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: The second-line drug [___] inhibits cell wall synthesis by acting as a structural analog of D-alanine, specifically targeting alanine racemase and D-alanyl-D-alanine ligase.
back:
Cycloserine
- Inhibits D-alanine incorporation into peptidoglycan
- Used exclusively for resistant tuberculosis
- Requires pyridoxine co-administration

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: A patient undergoing MDR-TB therapy develops acute psychosis, tremors, and convulsions. This adverse profile is characteristically associated with [___].
back:
Cycloserine
- Causes dose-related CNS toxicity
- Toxicity increases at peak levels >35 mcg/mL
- Ameliorated by pyridoxine (100mg+)

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Explain the biochemical mechanism by which Ethionamide disrupts the integrity of the Mycobacterium tuberculosis cell envelope.
back:
- Blocks mycolic acid synthesis
- Forms covalent complex with AcpM and KasA
- Acts similarly to isoniazid but retains activity in some INH-resistant strains

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Contrast Bedaquiline and Moxifloxacin regarding their shared high-yield cardiac adverse effect during multidrug-resistant tuberculosis treatment.
back:
- Both cause QTc interval prolongation
- Require baseline and periodic ECG monitoring
- High risk of fatal arrhythmias if used with other QTc-prolonging drugs

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Identify the primary biochemical target and the most common organ system affected by the adverse effects of Para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS).
back:
- Target: Folate synthesis (dihydropteroate synthase inhibition)
- Organ System: Gastrointestinal (nausea, vomiting, peptic ulceration, hemorrhage)

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: The second-line agent [___] is utilized for MDR-TB but requires careful monitoring due to risks of reversible bone marrow suppression and irreversible peripheral or optic neuropathy.
back:
Linezolid
- Inhibits protein synthesis (23S rRNA)
- Common side effect: Thrombocytopenia
- Avoid concurrent serotonergic agents (serotonin syndrome risk)

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: A patient with MDR-TB is prescribed an oral diarylquinoline. Ingestion with a [___] is required to significantly increase systemic drug exposure and efficacy.
back:
High-fat meal
- Refers to Bedaquiline
- Increases bioavailability approximately twofold
- Drug has extremely long half-life (5.5 months)

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Explain how Para-aminosalicylic acid (PAS) specifically inhibits the growth of Mycobacterium tuberculosis while sparing human cells.
back:
- Folate synthesis antagonist
- Competes with p-aminobenzoic acid (PABA)
- Selective because humans use exogenous folate and lack dihydropteroate synthase

category: Discuss 2nd line drugs used in treatment of multidrug resistant tuberculosis with their therapeutic and adverse effects
front: Contrast Amikacin and Streptomycin regarding their molecular mechanisms of resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
back:
